The Old Melbourne Gaol

Construction of the Old Melbourne Gaol began in 1839 and many extensions were added over the 
years to cope with the increasing numbers of prisoners. When it opened in 1845, it held fifty-nine 
men and nine women. 
1

approximately £20 000 in 1854. If £1 = $2, how much 
did the contractor receive to build the gaol in dollars? 
Convert this to find the dollar value in 2012.

P = reward, R = rate of inflation as a decimal and n is 
the number of years. Assume the rate of inflation has 
averaged 3.2% during this time.

Jack the Ripper	
5
Jack the Ripper is the most notorious serial killer in history. He is believed to be responsible for a 
number of murders in the slum areas around the Whitechapel district of London in 1888. The name 
‘Jack the Ripper’ originated in a letter, which was printed in the newspapers, written by someone 
claiming to be the murderer. Despite lengthy police investigations, the identity of the person who 
committed these crimes has never been discovered.

Espionage	
6
A spy is a person employed to gather secret information or to spread false information. This work 
is known as espionage. Spies may be employed by governments to gain an advantage over their 
enemies, or by other organisations for commercial benefit. A spy may spend years building a ‘normal’ 
identity to hide his or her undercover activities and learn many techniques to secretly communicate 
information.
Watta B. Blunder was a British scientist who was exposed as a Soviet spy. A timeline of the 
main events in his life is shown below.

Soviet Union? 
6

by the Soviets?

Have you ever sent a text message like ‘wot r u doin 2nite?’ If you have, then welcome to the world 
of secrecy, spies and espionage. Spies use complex codes and ciphers (a series of steps that decipher a 
certain code) to communicate secret information. Codes and ciphers have been around since the time 
of the Ancient Romans, and are one of the oldest forms of secret communication. Cryptography is 
the science of encoding and decoding secret messages.

James Bond, 007	
7
James Bond is a famous spy and is the main character in a large number of very popular action films. 
He is a fictional character created by Ian Fleming in 1953. Fleming wrote 12 novels and two short 
story collections featuring James Bond before he died in 1964. Other authors have since written 
James Bond stories. 
EON Productions hold the rights to produce the Bond films and have made many successful 
movies starring this character. The film series has grossed over $4 billion. When this figure 
is adjusted for inflation it is almost $11 billion. This means the Bond movies are the highest 
grossing film series ever, outdoing even Harry Potter.

Time of death

Pathology is the study of disease and cause of death. A forensic pathologist specialises in examining 
dead bodies to determine how and when death occurred.
When a dead body is discovered, one of the first priorities is to determine the time of death. 
The pathologist starts by taking the temperature of the body. The normal temperature inside 
a human body is 37°C. A pathologist will take the temperature inside the body, as well as the 
temperature of the location the body was discovered.

death.

Hoon drivers	
12
Many drivers cheat a little when driving. For example, they think that if the speed limit is 	
50 km/h, and they drive at 53 km/h they won’t be pulled over by police. So they happily let the 
speedometer hover just above the speed limit, even though they are breaking the law and greatly 
increasing their chances of crashing. 
1	
The stopping distance for a car is based on the driver’s reaction or thinking time to 
apply the brakes, and the actual braking distance for the car. Use the formulas below to 
calculate the total stopping distances, to one decimal place, for cars driving at various 
speeds.

Hoon driving can include doing ‘burn-outs’, racing cars on public land, ‘doughnuts’ in car 
parks and repeated instances of excessive speeding or driving without a licence. The public 
are also encouraged to ‘dob in a hoon’. Hoon drivers can have their vehicle impounded or, in

Maths in Crime & Espionage	
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011
Crash scenes	
13
The scientific process of investigating, analysing and drawing conclusions about the causes and 
events during a vehicle collision is carried out by vehicular accident reconstruction. 
Re-constructionists try to identify the causes of the crash. 
Forensic experts examine the skid marks at a 
crash scene as these can be used to determine 
an estimate for the speed that a vehicle was 
travelling. The formula used to calculate the 
speed of a car from skid to stop is given by: 
v =
255µS , where v is the speed in km/h, S is 
the length of the skid mark in metres and µ is the 
coefficient of friction.
1	
Calculate the speed that these cars were 
driving on a dry asphalt road, where 	µ = 0.7 
and the skid marks were measured to be:
a	 25 m	
b	 35 m 	
c	 45 m	
d	 5002 cm	
e	 20 m 35 cm.
2	
Calculate the speed that these cars were driving at on a wet asphalt road, where µ = 0.4 
and the skid marks were measured to be:
a	 20 m	
b	 31 m 	
c	 34 m	
d	 4 120 cm	
e	 15 m 45 cm.
If you were an Indianapolis race driver, you would use ‘slick’ racing tyres with no tread. On 
dry surfaces you might get as high as 0.9 as a coefficient of friction, but driving them on wet 
roads would be dangerous since the wet road coefficient might be as low as 0.1.
3	
Calculate the length of the skid mark an Indianapolis racing car would make on a dry 
asphalt track if it was travelling at:
a	 160 km/h	
b	 210 km/h	
c	 260 km/h	
d	 110 km/h	
e	 190 km/h.
4	
Calculate the length of the skid mark an Indianapolis racing car would make on a wet 
asphalt track if it was travelling at:
a	 160 km/h	
b	 210 km/h	
c	 260 km/h	
d	 110 km/h	
e	 190 km/h.
5	
Compare your answers for Q3 and Q4. What do you notice?
6	
A driver claimed her car was travelling just on the speed limit in a school zone. She 
braked and stopped only centimetres from a student on a crossing. Investigators at the 
scene found that weather conditions were fine and sunny and the road surface was 
asphalt. The car’s tyres were in excellent condition. They measured the skid marks of her 
car and found them to be 16 m long. Was she telling the truth? Explain your answer.
7	
The driver of a Toyota Camry failed to give way to the right at a small intersection in a 	
50 km/h zone. A Commodore hit the side of the Camry with a considerable amount of 
force. He claimed, as part of his defence, that the other car was travelling significantly 
over the speed limit. Forensics on the scene found that the road was very wet, and the skid 
marks of the car that was allegedly speeding were 95 m long. The tyres of the Commodore 
were in poor condition and resembled the ‘slicks’ of racing cars. Does the driver of the 
Camry have any defence? Explain your answer.

Blood stain analysis	
14
Forensics uses many other disciplines of science to assist in solving criminal cases. Blood stain 
pattern analysis (BPA) is a specialty within the field of forensic science. Recent scientific and 
technological advances have improved the use and application of blood stains as evidence.
Blood is a tissue that is circulated within the body to assist other parts of the body. Blood 
has specialised cells that allow it to carry out its complex functions. In a healthy person, 
approximately 8% of their total weight is blood.

Blood contains three components suspended within plasma. The three components are 
erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets. Plasma is a yellowish fluid composed of 92% water, 7% 
proteins and other materials such as salts and waste. Plasma makes up about 55% of blood. 
The remaining 45% is blood cells and platelets.

32	
Maths in Crime & Espionage	
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011
DNA	
15
DNA or deoxyribonucleic acid is found in the centre of almost all living cells. DNA is an incredibly 
long, thin strand of material about two metres in length, coiled inside each cell. Forensic scientists 
use DNA, such as in a strand of hair found at a crime scene, to identify matching DNA of another 
individual, such as the suspect. This process is called genetic fingerprinting. 
The following measurements were taken of the width of a DNA chain: 2.2, 2.4, 2.3, 2.2, 2.5 
and 2.6 nanometres.
1	
Calculate the average width of the DNA chain, in nanometres.
2	
A nanometre is one-billionth of a metre, that is, 	
1 × 10-9 m. Express your answer to Q1 in metres:
a	 as a decimal	
b	 in scientific notation.
A human DNA strand contains up to three billion base 
pairs, each pair being about 0.33 nanometres long. 
3	
Calculate the length of a human DNA strand. 
Write your answer in:
a	 nanometres	
b	 metres.
4	
The human body contains about 1014 cells. Each cell contains a DNA strand. Calculate 
the length of the entire DNA in the human body if it is lined up end to end. Write your 
answer in:
a	 nanometres	
b	 metres	
c	 kilometres.
5	
How many times would this DNA reach the moon, if the average distance of the moon to 
Earth is 384 400 km?
6	
How many times around the Earth would this DNA stretch if the diameter of the Earth is 
12 576 km?
7	
One of the great things about a DNA fingerprint is that it can be stored easily in 
computers. In the United States, the FBI has 5 million DNA profiles of convicts and over 
200 000 profiles of DNA crime scenes. The population of the US is about 308 367 000. 
Calculate as a percentage of the total population the DNA profiles the FBI has:
a	 collected from convicts	
b	 of crime scenes.
8	
In one country, 30 000 DNA samples are processed each year, each one taking just 5 days 
to analyse. If the population of this country is 34 036 000 people, calculate:
a	 the number of DNA samples processed per week
b	 the total amount of time, in years, it has taken to process these DNA samples.
9	
In one European country the DNA database grows at about 400 000 per year. Everyone 
arrested even for a minor crime has their DNA profile analysed. The population of this 
country is around 62 784 500 people.

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011	
Maths in Crime & Espionage	
33
DNA (cont’d)	
15
a	 Round off the population to the nearest million.
b	 Calculate the percentage growth per year of DNA profiles.
c	 At this rate, how long would it take to have a DNA profile for the entire population?

individuals in 15 murder cases and 31 rapes every month.
a	 If there are 160 rapes per month, in what percentage of cases is DNA being used to 
identify the perpetrator?
b	 If there are 17 murders per month, in what percentage of cases is DNA being used to 
identify the murderer?
DNA is constructed using four different building bases: Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine and Guanine. 
DNA stores information about the individuals in a code created by the sequence of these bases. Much 
of the DNA appears to be junk. The length of these stretches of ‘junk’ DNA varies from person to 
person to form a genetic fingerprint of that person. Scientists use a process of electrophoresis to 
map the stretches of ‘junk’ DNA to produce a DNA profile, the result of which looks like a barcode 
found on supermarket goods.
11	 Make a list of some common sources of DNA at a crime scene.
Matching DNA from a crime scene to DNA taken from a suspect is not an absolute guarantee 
of the suspect’s guilt. Instead, forensic experts prefer to talk about probability of a DNA match. 
DNA is made up of four different bases: Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G) and 	
Thymine (T).

Maths in Crime & Espionage	
© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011
Fingerprints	
16
Experts have come to believe that each person’s fingerprints are unique, even those of identical 
twins. The probability of two people having the same fingerprint is more than one in sixty billion. 
Experts start comparing fingerprints by examining the core of the prints. The core can be 
one of three patterns: arch, loop or whorl. Once they have identified the basic core type of 
fingerprint, the characteristics (minutiae) of the ridges are compared. Some of these minutiae 
are shown in the table below.

ending
Dot
Lake
Bifurcation
Spur

Trifurcation

d	 five characteristics in common.

matches a fingerprint found at the scene of the 
crime, what can the experts conclude?
5

fingerprint that match a fingerprint found at 
the scene of a crime, fingerprint experts will be 
confident the suspect was at the scene. Why is this?

Ballistics

A bullet is a projectile propelled by a rifle or handgun. Many people believe that bullets fly in a 
straight line. This is untrue, they travel in a parabolic trajectory – one that becomes more and more 
curved as the distance the bullet travels increases. The centre line of the bore (the inner diameter 
of the gun barrel) is angled slightly upward in relation to the line of the sights (which are above the 
bore) so that the projectile crosses the line of sight on its way up and again on its way down.  
The Ballistic 
Coefficient (BC) 
is basically a 
measure of how 
streamlined a 
bullet is; that is, 
how well it cuts 
through the air.

air.

Graffiti	
18
Graffiti is the act of marking a property or wall, without the consent of the owner, with writing, 
symbols or drawings. Graffiti is illegal and is a persistent problem in almost all towns and cities. 
The main motivators for graffiti artists are fame, adrenaline rush, artistic expression and malicious 
damage.
In one year approximately 14 000 incidents of graffiti were reported to police.

a	 twenty-six percent took place at residential properties

Cyberbullying	
19
Cyberbullying is when a person is harassed or threatened by another person or group of people 
using technology like the Internet and mobile phones. Young people are particularly vulnerable to 
this type of hostile behaviour. They may receive text or email messages that contain hurtful and 
embarrassing comments or threats. Cyberbullies may also use social networking sites to start 
gossip or disclose private information about another person. 
A research study discovered that over 60% of students were victims of cyberbullying.
1

students?

b	 249

d	 491

have been threatened more than once. How

those 58% students, more than four out of ten said it happened more than once. How 
many students have received:
a	 hurtful messages online?	
b	 hurtful messages more than once? 
6	
Fifty-six percent of students have not told their parents they have received hurtful 
messages online. How many students is this? 
7

Therefore, determine the statistical extent of cyberbullying in your classroom. 
8

Environmental crime

 The world is now facing numerous environmental challenges and threats. Environmental crime, 
including illegal trading of natural resources and dumping of hazardous waste, is a serious and 
growing international problem. As the world’s natural resources rapidly diminish, environmental 
crimes such as illegal logging and fishing are increasing and are billion dollar activities.
In 1989 the oil tanker Exxon Valdez ran aground on Bligh Reef, spewing vast amounts of oil 
into the ocean.
1	
The tanker carried almost 240 million litres of oil. Fifty million litres of this oil spilled into 
the ocean. 
a	 What was the fraction of oil that spilled into the ocean?	
b	 What is this fraction as a percentage?
c	 What percentage of oil did not spill into the ocean?
2	
Alaska has a coastline of approximately 6000 miles.
a	 How many kilometres is this if 1 mile is the same as 1.61 
kilometres?
b	 1300 miles of the shoreline was polluted by oil. How 
many kilometres is this?
c	 What fraction of the coastline was polluted?
d	 What percentage of the coastline was not polluted?
3	
Approximately 35 000 birds and 1000 sea otters were confirmed to be dead after the spill.
a	 What is the total number of dead animals found?  
b	 What fraction were sea otters?	
c	 What percentage were birds?
4	
Since most of the dead sank into the water, it was 
estimated that the total number killed was 250 000 
seabirds, 2800 sea otters, 300 harbor seals, 250 bald 
eagles, 22 killer whales, and billions of salmon and 
herring eggs. Disregarding the fish, make estimates 
based on the figures above of the: 
a	 total number of birds and animals killed	
	
b	 fraction (decimal) of sea birds killed	
c	 fraction of sea otters killed	
	
d	 percentage of harbour seals killed	
e	 percentage of birds killed.
f	 Draw a column graph on the axes provided to 
display the loss of animals (do not include sea 
birds).
5	
Exxon was fined $150 million. Since Exxon cooperated in the massive clean-up and also 
paid private claims, the court forgave $125 million. The remaining $25 million was split 
between the North American Wetlands Conservation Fund and the national Victims of 
Crime Fund.

© Denis Day and Blake Education 2011	
Maths in Crime & Espionage	
43
Environmental crime (cont’d)	
20
a	 What is the decimal fraction for the amount the court forgave Exxon?
b	 What is this amount as a percentage?
6	
Exxon also paid $100 million to federal and state governments for environmental 
projects. Exxon also agreed to a $900 million settlement in a civil agreement. The 	
$900 million went to pay for further environmental projects. 
a	 Find the total amount, in billions of dollars, that Exxon had to pay for the oil spill. 
Don’t forget the fines.
b	 What fraction was given to federal and state governments for environmental projects?
Serious organised crime in the forestry and timber industries is one of the most pressing environmental 
issues facing the global community. Significant volumes of natural resources are harvested, sold, purchased, 
transported or exported using illegal methods. The proceeds of illegal logging are laundered in the Asia–Pacific 
region, fostering corruption and undermining environmental governance.
7	
Illegal forestry is directly linked to climate change as around one-fifth of global 
greenhouse gas emissions are linked to forest loss.
a	 Express the amount of illegal forestry linked to climate change as a decimal fraction.
b	 What is this fraction as a percentage?
8	
Indonesia has the highest rate of deforestation in the world, at almost two million 
hectares each year. How many hectares is this per:
a	 month?	
b	 week?	
c	 day?	
d	hour?
9	
A football field is approximately 2 hectares in size. How many football fields of forest are 
being cleared per hour in Indonesia?
10	 Satellite images show that 60 million hectares of Indonesia’s forests are in a severely 
damaged state. How many equivalent football fields of forest is this?
11	 A recent report has revealed that illegal logging is taking place in 37 out of Indonesia’s 41 
national parks.
a	 Express the number of national parks not being logged as a decimal fraction.
b	 What is the percentage of parks being logged?
12	 Reports state that predatory loggers in Papua are illegally smuggling up to 300 000 
cubic metres of merbau logs a month to China’s booming wooden flooring industry. If a 
merbau tree produces 5 cubic metres of timber, how many merbau trees are being logged 
in a:
a	 month?	
	 	
b	 day (assume 30 days per month)?		
c	 year?	
	 	
d	 week?
13	 It is estimated that the local community in Papua receives $11 per cubic metre for the 
timber, the Papuan exporter receives $120 and the Chinese importer receives $240. The 
manufactured price in China is $468 and the retail price in imported countries such as 
the UK, US and Australia is $2300. Calculate the total cost paid per cubic metre, then the 
percentage amount at each stage.

Event fact and fiction 
1
History is full of interesting information about events. Events can be social functions, dinners, 
sporting events, award nights, fetes, launches and ‘-thons’, such as walkathons. In Australia,  
special events are often used to promote travel and tourism too. 
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer. 
1 
As more companies developed events over the last 5 years in Australia, the amounts 
raised after costs showed an 85% growth to $2.8 million. How much in whole number 
dollars was raised through events 5 years ago?  
Idea: x × 1.85 = 2.8 million
Special events
2 
It was suggested that the full Greek national anthem be 
sung at the opening of the Olympic Games in Athens 
in 2004. How many verses are said to be in the Greek 
national anthem?  
Idea: (the area of a square of side length 12 units) – 4
3

Woodstock Music Festival, held on a 2 400 000 m2 farm in 
the United States. Six hundred toilets were provided.
a How many square metres per person were available?
b How many people per toilet were there? Give your answer as a whole number.
4 
The opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge was a grand event with fireworks, a parade of 
floats and marching bands. 
a How many years did it take to build the bridge? 
Idea: (the area of a triangle with base length 
2 units and height 8 units)
b How many people watched the opening, 
when a horseman cut the ribbon ahead of 
Premier Lang?  
Idea: 36 million ÷ 480
c In what year was the opening? 
Idea: 2 × 32 × 102 + 11 × 22 × 3

to the nearest million.

women play netball every month?  
Idea: 182 535 + 77 465 – 20 000
7 
Many international hockey tournaments are hosted in Australia. For how many years has 
hockey been played?  
Idea: 90	000

Big events, big money 
2
Many events involve paying big money to movie stars and other celebrities to help promote the 
occasion. These stars can influence the success of the event. This is particularly true of big events in 
areas such as sport and entertainment. Big numbers have lots of numbers and zeros, and you have to 
be careful that you don’t make silly mistakes.
1 
Using 1s and 0s, write the answer to 1 million + 
1 billion + 1 trillion + 1 quintillion + 1 sextillion 
+ 1 nonillion.
2 
A googol is a 1 with a hundred zeros. Write a 
googol as a power of 10.
3 
A googolplex is the biggest number with a 
name. A googolplex is 1 with googol zeros. Write 
a googolplex as powers of 10.
money, money, money
4 
Convention centres are used for events such 
as trade fairs and conferences. In 2005 in the 
United States, $2.4 billion was spent building  
44 new centres. How much did each centre cost 
on average? Give you answer correct to the 
nearest whole number.
5 
A state events development program has 
invested $9.7 million in 460 events since it began

on average? Give your answer correct to the

to play in a local tournament, one of the state governments agreed to pay half of his  
$4.5 million appearance fee. 
a How many million dollars did the government pay Panther?  
b The government stated that Panther’s appearance would generate $19 million in 
economic benefits. What is the government’s payment as a percentage of the estimated 
economic benefits? Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
c A sample of 500 people was asked whether the state government should contribute to 
Panther’s fee: 65% said ‘no’. How many people said ‘no’ to the question?
7

he should be paid just ¾ of that figure. How much did they think he should be paid?
8

keen to become involved. Peter Pitchen, a star player, recently signed a contract 
worth $250 million. There are 1200 players in the competition. If every player in 
the competition was to receive the same amount as Peter, how much would this cost 
altogether? What is this amount in trillion dollars?

Charities organise events that raise money for good causes. Charitable foundations are good

12,	you	need	1.25	m2	per	guest.

There are risks in managing an event: risks to human life, the environment, the organisation 
hosting the event, the operation or project, and to the reputations of the organisation and other 
people. It is important to insure against some eventualities and to prepare for others.
Be insured!
1 
At least 5% of the entire budget for an event 
should be allowed for unforeseen happenings. If 
the entire budget for a street fair is $25 000, how 
much should be allowed for emergencies?
2 
a An insurance company earned $4 million 
in premiums and paid out only $200 000 to 
victims of accidents. What percentage of the 
premiums was paid to victims?
b How much profit did the insurance company 
make? 
3 
A school fete had 15 market stalls and the 
organisers needed to insure each stall separately. 
a The organisers must take out public liability 
insurance to cover any injuries to people 
who attend the fete. The minimum insurance 
premium for each stall is $255 for $10 million 
cover. How much will it cost for all the stalls?
b The organisers must also take out product liability insurance to cover any injury caused 
by what they are selling. The minimum insurance premium for each stall is $110 for  
$10 million cover. How much will this cost for all the stalls?
c How much will the insurance cost altogether?
4 
Entertainers such as musicians, clowns, puppeteers and 
face-painters must be insured. For $10 million cover, the 
premiums vary as shown in the table, right.
a Action Entertainment will provide a fair with 2 solo 
singers, 1 face-painter, a magician double act and a 
10-person puppet group. How much will insurance cost?
b If the performers are required to share the insurance 
cost equally, how much must each pay?
5 
Between 2010 and 2012, the average claim on events 
public liability insurance at Ecco Insurance Company 
(EIC) increased from $55 000 to $88 000. 
a By what percentage did the average claim change 
between 2010 and 2012?
b EIC wants to put up its premiums in 2013, using the 
same annual rate of change as the average claim over 
2010–12. If the average premium in 2012 was $225,  
what should be the premium in 2013?
risky business

Product	liability	insurance	is	a	policy	
that	covers	you	for	any	injury	or	damage	
caused	by	a	product	you	supply.

promising weather
The weather can be the difference between 
an event’s success or failure. Forecasting 
the chance of rain is very difficult, since the 
probability of rain usually changes from day 
to day. 
6 
The probability that it will rain during 
Saturday’s walkathon is said to be 20%. 
What is the probability that the weather 
will be fine?
7 
Philip’s Event Company is running 
an outdoor art show from Monday 
to Friday, inclusive. If it rains, the 
show will be ruined. Philip asks a 
weather forecaster the probability 
that it will rain some time during 
Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, 
Thursday or Friday. He is told that 
at this time of the year every day 
has a 15% probability of rain. 
a What is the probability that it 
won’t rain on a particular day? 
Call this q and express it as a 
percentage.
b The way to work out the 
probability of no rain during the 
show is to calculate:
 100% – q × q × q × q × q = 
100% –          % =          % 
 Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
We can’t afford it!
Sponsors are interested in how much they can earn from 
their investment in your event. You need to prove that 
you will be able to give them effective advertising of their 
product. However, it can be a risk to rely on sponsorship 
alone to run an event. Promises of sponsorship may not 
be kept!
8 
For the Boomers Expo, sponsorship is available at three levels: gold, costing $30 000; 
silver, costing $10 000; bronze, costing $5 000. Only 4 bronze, 4 silver and 1 gold 
sponsorships are available. 
a How much will the organisers receive if all the sponsorships are taken up?
b How much will organisers lose if the gold and 2 of the silver sponsorship promises are 
not kept?

free	attendance.

launching a book 
5
Alex and Ellie have written books on the importance of Mathematics in a number of occupations. 
Their latest  book is about event management and they decide that they should manage an event 
to launch the book. They have a small budget so they need to keep costs to a minimum. They have 
plenty of time and will do much of the work themselves. 
What about the date?

A book takes a long time from when 
it is first written until it arrives at the 
warehouse, ready to go to the shops. A 
book launch will be booked the day the 
manuscript is delivered to the publisher. 
The launch will be held the day that the

A quiz show needs to be organised like any other event. The manager needs to work out the theme 
of the quiz, how many contestants will participate, who will be in the audience, how long the show 
will last and what the prizes will be.

how long is the show?

There will be 6 contestants. How much time on average will each contestant have to 
answer questions?

appearance money. After the first round

how many people will be in the audience?

the audience. It is decided to have 6 contestants selected from the audience. 
a What percentage of people in the auditorium are women?
b The sponsor of the quiz is Kleen washing powder. They want the first contestant on the 
show to be a woman. What is the chance that this will be the case?

Farewell for Frances 
8
Frances is the principal of Fairview High School. She has been at the school for a very long time 
and will retire soon. All the parents want to give her a farewell party and there is a great deal of 
discussion about what kind of party to have.
1 
Frances leaves on the afternoon of 21 December. It is already 1 October, so the parents 
consult the calendar.
a The parents have decided that the best nights for the party would be Friday or Saturday 
night. How many choices do they have for the party if they do not wish to hold it on 
Frances’ last night?
b If they need at least 5 weeks to plan the party, what is the earliest date the party could 
be held?
c If they hold the party on the last Saturday before Frances leaves, how many days will 
the parents have to prepare?
2 
The school will allow a party to be held in its large assembly hall, with 450 people for 
3 hours. It has the advantage that there would be no venue charge. The music would also 
be free because the school band can play, and the parents only need to provide drinks 
and food. There would be a charge of $8 per hour per person for drinks. How much, in 
total, would it cost for drinks? 
3 
One of the parents has offered to make platters of canapés, the small appetising ‘finger 
foods’ that are easy to eat standing up. Each canapé will cost $2 and each guest is

Big yachting event 
9
The world over, yachting is considered to be a thrilling sport. A series of yacht races is called a 
regatta. Regattas are big events that require a great deal of organisation. In this unit, plans are to 
be made for a 120-km yacht race around the Greek Islands.
Safety boat
1 
There must be a safety plan for any yacht race event. First aid, fresh water, fuel, 
life-saving equipment and the weather need to be considered. There is usually a  
safety boat, which is the only motorboat allowed near the yachts!
a In the race, 12 yachts are expected to each carry 4 people. How many people will be 
sailing around the Greek Islands?
b If each person consumes 750 mL of fresh water every 4 hours, how many litres of fresh 
water are consumed by the sailors during an 8-hour journey?
c The safety boat usually has a 2-stroke motor. For this motor, the fuel mix is made from 
1 litre of oil to every 50 litres of petrol. 
 i If 50 litres of petrol are used in the fuel mix, how many litres of boat fuel are 
 
produced?
 ii How much oil in mL is required to make 21 litres of fuel mix?
d If 1.67 litres of fuel enables the safety boat to travel 1 km, how much fuel is required for 
the 120-km race?
Sailing through the numbers!
The managers of the race require the organisers to plot the 
positions of the yachts on a chart as they sail through the 
course. The race starts at Delos, heads to Mykonos, then 
Naxos and then back to Delos. The charts are in nautical 
miles, so plotting the sailing course often requires the 
conversion of kilometres to nautical miles. 
2 
a Use Fast Moving Facts to convert 120 km into nautical 
miles. Give your answer correct to 3 decimal places.
b Speeds are expressed as nautical miles per hour or knots. The yachts average a speed of 
10 knots. What is 10 knots in km per hour? 
c How long will the race take if the yachts average 10 knots? 
 i Give the answer in hours to 4 decimal places.
 ii Give your answer in hours and minutes.
3

boat is 5 nautical miles away when it receives  
a ‘mayday’ emergency call from Dee’s Devil 
reporting that one of the crew has fallen  
overboard. The temperature of the water is 
estimated to be 6°C, and the safety boat can  
travel at a speed of 20 knots. Use the graph to  
find if the crew member will be unconscious  
when the safety boat reaches him.

See-More High School in Melbourne, Australia, is arranging a Science study tour to the Great 
Barrier Reef, off the north-eastern coast of Australia. Twenty Year 12 students along with two 
teachers will fly between Melbourne and Cairns airports. The objective of the study tour is to 
investigate and report on a series of coral formations and other marine life.
ready, set, jet!
The flights between Melbourne and Cairns will be aboard the AirAustralia airline. 
1 
a The plane is part of the 737-500 series fleet. The total 
passenger seating capacity for the aircraft is 200, 15% of 
which are seats allocated to Premier Class. How many 
seats on board the vessel are in Economy Class?
b The usual Melbourne–Cairns return airfare in Economy 
Class is $150, including taxes. The Economy seats on 
the flight are fully booked. Use your answer to Question 
1a to calculate AirAustralia’s revenue from this flight’s 
Economy Class fares.
c Premier Class seats on the Melbourne–Cairns return 
flight cost an additional 30%. Calculate AirAustralia’s 
revenue from this class.
d Calculate AirAustralia’s sales for the round trip to Cairns for all seats.
e The estimated travelling time from Melbourne to Cairns is 3 hours at a typical cruising 
speed of 835 km per hour. Calculate the distance travelled for the round trip in kilometres.
What do you mean I am overweight?
2 
a Economy Class passengers on the Cairns flight are each allowed 20 kg of cargo luggage 
and 7 kg of carry-on luggage. If there are 170 Economy Class passengers, what is the 
maximum mass of cargo luggage for all Economy Class?
b What is the total mass of carry-on luggage permitted for all Economy Class seats?
c The Premier Class ticket price is 30% more than an Economy Class ticket of $150. How 
much is a Premier Class ticket? 
d Every kilogram that an Economy ticket holder’s luggage is overweight incurs an 
excess luggage fee of 5% of the cost of a Premier Class ticket. Two students, Jessica and 
Cameron, have packed too much! Jessica has an additional 4 kg and Cameron has an 
additional 5.5 kg. How much will they each have to pay for excess luggage if they are 
both travelling Economy Class?
the sleeper!
AirAustralia has introduced a new plane, the 777-300 series, to complement its existing fleet. This 
plane seats 350 passengers. Economy Class has 260 seats, Premier Class has 50 seats and First 
Class, renamed the ‘Sleeper’, has 40 seats. This new series costs 15% more for the Melbourne–
Cairns return flight in Economy Class than the $150 charged on the old 737-500 series.
3 
a Calculate how much AirAustralia could receive in return fares if all the Melbourne–
Cairns Economy Class seats on the new 777-300 series are sold.
ready, set, dive!

going to the tivoli 
11
Aaron has just been appointed as Event Manager for the Tivoli cinema chain. To be successful as an 
event manager, he must promote the 8 cinemas as venues for business functions, children’s parties 
and social groups. He decides to produce a folder of information that he can display at the cinemas 
and give to prospective customers. He must work out the contents of the folder and how much the 
promotion is going to cost before his boss will let him go ahead.
1 
There is an international standard for sizes of paper, and these 
paper sizes have the same ratio of height to width: 2 . The basic 
size is a sheet of paper measuring 1 m2, which is called A0. The 
next paper sizes in the series are called A1, A2, A3, etc., and are 
made by halving the preceding paper size parallel to its shorter 
side. In the diagram, right, A0 is the whole sheet, measuring 
1189 mm by 841 mm.
a Find the ratio of height to width for A0 paper, correct to 3 
decimal places.
b Find the dimensions of A2 paper and find the ratio of height 
to width. Give your answer 
correct to 3 decimal places.
c Based on your answer 
to Question 1b, find the 
dimensions of A4 paper. 
d An A0 sheet of paper 
measuring 1 m2 weighs 80 
grams. Express the area of 
an A4 sheet as a fraction of 
the area of an A0 sheet and 
thus find the weight of an 
A4 sheet of the same paper. 
e An A4-sized picture is 
reduced to A5 size. What is 
the percentage reduction 
in area?
2 
To advertise movies available for business functions, Aaron will include one A4 leaflet 
inside each of his 500 folders. He will use 80 gsm paper. Use Fast Paper and Card Facts 
and the area of an A4 sheet to find the mass of 
the 500 sheets.
3

folded in half so that the folder is A4 size. 
a What are the dimensions of the cardboard 
used to make a folder?
b What area of cardboard is needed for a 
folder in:

The Alpha-Clubs Championship was held at the Aurora Stadium last night. It was an exciting game 
and the sponsors and both clubs were very happy with the event.
1 
The Aurora Stadium was the first choice for the organisers of the championship for the 
reasons below. Use the calculations to find out the facts about the stadium.
a It can hold (9 × 6 – 1) × 103 fans.
b There are 52 × 102 undercover car parks 
available.
c The area of the arena is 23 × 52 × 102 square 
metres. 
d There are 102 × 103 × 104
10 × 102 × 103  television monitors
 for business guests.
e (52 – 3 × 2) × 106 people have attended the 
Aurora Stadium since it opened in the year 
2000.
2 
Use the Fast Soccer Field Facts and the area of the Aurora Stadium arena from Question 
1c to find out if the area of the arena is likely to be large enough for:
a a local soccer match 
b an international soccer match.
3 
a The crowd at the Alpha-Clubs Championship game was 53 273, in a stadium seating 
52 500; the rest needed to stand. How many fans needed to stand?
b Regulations state that for every 5000 people or part thereof, the organisers need 
to provide 6 toilets, 25 urinals and 17 washbasins for men and 34 toilets and  
17 washbasins for women. List the toilet facilities required for the game.
4 
An overview of the key features of the game will be reported on the TV news. This will be 
good advertising for the event.
a The Alpha-Clubs Championship game began at 7.30 pm. Both teams finished the 
match 90 minutes later, each with only 10 men on the field. At what time did the game 
finish?
b In the 20th minute of the 
match Billy, playing for the 
Reds, scored the only goal of 
the match. At what time did 
Billy score the goal?
c In the 10th minute of the 
match Angelo, playing for the 
Blues, was sent off after hitting 
Georgio, who was playing for 
the Reds. Then Georgio was 
sent off at the 65th minute. For 
how long did the Reds have 
more players on the field than 
the Blues?
Bending the ball! 
12

•

5 
The Aurora Stadium has a number of function rooms used for different activities, as listed 
in the table, below. Use the table to answer the following questions.
a Which area will allow the greatest number of guests in a theatre function?
b Which room would need to be used for a banquet for 1160 guests?
c Which area would be best for a small banquet of fewer that 50 people?

because it is part of 600 years of naval tradition and history. Sometimes there is also a Blessing of 
the Fleet, like those used to call for good fishing and a safe return for fishermen.

Promoters are organising an annual event in Australia called Fashion Week. This important event 
is to promote existing and new fashion designers to buyers from all over the world. During Fashion 
Week, parades are conducted and display stands are fitted out to best show and promote fashion 
collections. This year’s Fashion Week is themed ‘Botany’, as a way of emphasising the importance of 
the environment. Eco-friendly products are used throughout the exhibition centre.
Showing off!

‘thread’ in Italian. The WonderDome is hosting this prestigious event. Six runways allow 
fashion houses to display their designs.

fashion purchase amount?

each with a capacity to seat 600 per day, are available. Calculate the total number of 
guests that could sit across all runways per day.

of each of the 4500 fashion buyers.

36	
Maths	in	Event	Management	
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2010
Staging an art exhibition is often a major event for an artist, a gallery and a community. Art 
galleries are generally located in major cities and key regional centres. Important shows are often 
exhibited internationally as a way of exchanging ideas between countries.
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, complete the calculations in it to find the answer. 
Ivana paintalot
Gallery Praxis in Sydney, Australia, has negotiated with 
modern artist Ivana Paintalot to exhibit at their gallery 
for their June show. 
1 
a A catalogue showcasing Ivana’s work has been 
produced, including an essay about her work by 
a specialist writer. The cost price to the gallery for 
each catalogue is $9.50. The gallery sells each for 
$14.95. What would the profit be if 500 were sold? 
b There are 16 two-metre square oil paintings and 
12 one-metre square charcoal drawings. The retail 
price for the two different forms are $8250 each 
and $3450 each respectively. 
 i Calculate the possible revenue to the gallery if 
 
all the paintings and works on paper are sold.
 ii What percentage of the possible revenue is 
 
expected from the works on paper? Give your  
 
answer correct to 3 decimal places.
 
c i   All the works on paper were sold and the gallery charged 20% of the wall price to 
    frame each of the works. How much does the gallery receive for the framing?
 ii The cost price to the gallery to frame each work on paper is $350. Calculate the 
 
gallery’s profit on framing.
d i   If 3 
4  of Ivana’s paintings and 2 
3  of the works on paper were sold, how much would 
    the gallery receive for the sales?
 ii Gallery Praxis pays the artist 60% of the retail price, excluding the framing charges. 
 
Calculate Ivana’s payment on these sales.
rodney mcClick
For the July show, Gallery Praxis is exhibiting Rodney McClick, a young modern photographer. 
2 
Gallery Praxis has approximately 800 people on its mailing list, of which 20% are 
overseas clients. The artist’s list is 30% of the size of the gallery’s list and everyone is local. 
a How many invitations could be sent if the gallery combines its list with that of the artist?
b How many invitations are being sent to overseas patrons? 
c Rodney McClick has produced 40 photographs of the Australian outback. The works are 
priced at $1750 each. Rodney sells 70% of his images off the wall. 
 i How much was received from sales?
 ii If the gallery pays him 60% of that value, how much money did Rodney earn?
modern art 
17

own	the	works	they	exhibit.
•

to	exhibit	and	sell	the	works	on	
behalf	of	the	artist	or	artists.	
•	
The	person	who	arranges	the	
gallery	space	is	called	the	curator.	
•	
The	retail	price	of	a	painting	is	
referred	to	as	the	wall	price.

37
d If another 30% of Rodney’s images were sold as extra editions and the gallery makes 
40% commission on these, calculate the gallery’s commission on these additional sales.
The opening night of an exhibition is an important marketing event for the gallery and the 
artist. Generally 1 in 3 of the combined local mailing lists will attend the opening night. 
Knowing this helps plan the evening. 
e Calculate the likely whole number of patrons attending the opening night.
f If approximately 5% of the guests attending the opening night purchase an image: 
 i what whole number of people will purchase an image? 
 ii how much money would Rodney make after the gallery took its 40% commission?
Freight on board! 
Gallery Praxis showcases artworks on their website for international promotion and purchase. 
The works are priced at $1750 each.
3 
a Of the 160 overseas people on their mailing list, 15% purchased an artwork.
 i How much money was received from the sales?
 ii How much did the gallery make if it receives 40% commission?
b A freight company will send 5 of the works to New York, 5 to London and 5 to 
Singapore. The freight rate to New York is $110 per piece, 8% less than that for London 
and 15% less than the London figure for Singapore. How much will it cost the gallery to 
send the 15 works?
c What percentage of the gallery’s commission does this international freight represent? 
Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
the young artist award Dinner
Gallery Praxis and ArtAust have arranged a gala dinner, with entertainment and keynote 
speakers, to raise funds for the Young Artist Achievement Awards (YAAA). Government 
dignitaries, fine art institutes and Arts patrons have been invited, a total of 350 guests. 
4 
a What was the total income raised by the gala dinner? 
Idea: 14.9 × 144 ÷ 6 × 7.5 × 350
b If the cost to produce the dinner and manage 
the event cost $111.75 per guest, calculate 
how much money is left to fund the YAAA.
c Three awards are being offered: one for 
painting, one for sculpture and one for 
photography. The award for painting is  
$10 000, the one for sculpture is 200% of 
that value and the award for photography is 
25% of the award for sculpture. Calculate the 
value of each award.
d The balance of the money is donated to 
the YAAA fund. What percentage does  
that represent? Give your answer correct to  
2 decimal places.

38	
Maths	in	Event	Management	
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2010
Street fairs and festivals are an exciting way for local communities to get together while promoting 
cultural diversity, music, film, food, and local arts and crafts. The budget for a street fair may be 
covered by the state government, the council and local shopkeepers, with the rest coming from 
sponsorship, donations and other activities. 
Windsor Street Festival
1 
a This year the 10-day festival of concerts, films and exhibitions has a budget of 
$1.2 million. The event organisers have applied to the state government for 35%  
of the project budget. Calculate this figure.
b Local traders have agreed to contribute an equivalent of 80% of the government’s 
contribution. How much money will come from the traders?
c The festival is over 4 street blocks in Windsor Street. It closes with a street fair, held from 
8 am to 11 pm on the last Sunday. The 8 food stalls in each street block will be charged 
a rent of $1680 for the day. What is the total rent money received for all 4 blocks?
d There will be a $2.50 parking day pass for those who drive to the festival. Calculate the 
amount of money that could be raised if 2200 car places are provided every day. 
e Calculate how much extra sponsorship money would need to be raised in order to meet 
the forecasted budget.
It’s all for a worthy cause!
GLOSS hair products are offering a free haircare 
show and on-stage hair demonstrations in return 
for their logo appearing on all festival materials. 
GLOSS will be the festival’s major sponsor.
2 
a What is the cost to GLOSS if they provide 
5000 free haircare showbags worth $12 each?
b The organisers have decided that they need 
$400 000 in sponsorship. GLOSS has agreed 
that their contribution will be 37.5% of this 
figure. Calculate GLOSS’s total sponsorship 
contribution, excluding the showbags.
c Universal night club and the UDance 
club will each contribute 12% of the total 
sponsorship in exchange for their logos 
and advertisements being used in the 
festival brochure and on signs in the street. 
Calculate their total contribution.
d Radio4U2 will be exclusively covering 
the 10-day festival activities in various 
languages. They are expecting $2.5 million of advertiser income, of which they have 
agreed to contribute 2% to the festival. How much money is that?
e Protect Technologies are providing 4 large digital screens (with their logo) playing 
music videos continuously for the day of the street fair, from 8 am until 11 pm. Their 
sponsorship is worth $1500 per hour. How much money is that?
f How much more sponsorship money is left to raise?
all is fair in the streets! 
18
© Blake Education   ISBN  978 1 92571 018 2	
    Maths in Event Management

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2010	
Maths	in	Event	Management	
39
programming
A programme will be produced and slipped into the local paper so that people will know 
what the different events are and when they will be on. The graphic design students of a local 
university have arranged the layout and artwork for the programmes at no charge.
3 
a The cost to print one 12-page programme is $6.25. A 
4-page programme costs 60% of the cost of a 12-page 
programme. How much will it cost to print a 4-page 
programme?
b Usually there are special rates for printing big orders 
of event programmes. The festival organisers order 
5250 of the 12-page programmes. Use Fast Printing 
Facts to calculate the printing cost.
c What would have been the printing cost if an extra 
1000 of the 12-page programmes had been ordered.
d The organisers decide they will need 10 000 of the 
4-page programmes to put in the newspapers. They 
are offered a printing cost of $1.74 per programme. 
 i What percentage of the cost of a 12-page programme is this?
 ii How much will these programmes cost?
e Calculate the total cost to the festival organisers if 6250 of the 12-page programmes are 
ordered along with 10 000 of the 4-page programmes?
f What would it have cost the festival organisers for all these programmes if they had not 
got the special prices for the big orders? 
g Calculate how much money has been saved because of special prices for big orders.
Screens all right to me!
Windsor Street has a large cinema, called M-Screen, running for 5 days of the festival. 
4 
a If M-Screen seats 1440 guests at each of the 5 films shown each day, calculate the 
number of people that M-Screen could seat for the period.
b The adult ticket price is $8 and those under 16 years of age pay $5 per ticket. If ¾ of 
the people found in Question 4a are paying the full price, how much money would be 
made from those 16 years of age and under?
c i   Assuming an 80% capacity for each session is achieved (of which ¾ paid full price), 
calculate the amount of money returned from sales of tickets. 
 ii Hence, how much is paid to the festival organisers if they receive 7% of total sales?
5 
A portable movie screen has been installed at the other end of the street to provide 
open-air movie screenings. The open-air movie shows will comprise 2 movies per night  
for 3 nights, half of which are foreign films. 650 people are expected at each film.
a Calculate the expected ticket sales for all the foreign films if all tickets cost $6.50.
b $1.50 will be paid to festival organisers from each ticket sold. Calculate how much 
money will be paid to the festival organisers if the expected open-air movie numbers 
are achieved.

A variety of merchandise is usually available as part of local, national or international events. This 
helps promoters and event managers to raise money to pay for special guests or for the event itself.
Badge of honour
A soccer club held a game in Brisbane for which satin badges were sold to help promote the 
soccer grand final.
1 
The Club bought 10 000 satin badges for $2.45 each and sold each for $4. All the badges 
were sold. If the profit is the difference between the amount received from sales and the 
amount the badges cost, how much profit was made by the club altogether?
Some hair-raising sales!
To coincide with the opening of their renovated salons, the owners of Ecco Hairdressing 
wanted to thank their loyal customers with free tickets to the Three Divas Concert in the Park. 
2

holders. The tickets were priced at $55 each.
a How much did Ecco Hairdressing pay 
for all its tickets if they received a 20% 
discount on the selling price?
b The venue holds 6120 people. How 
much did the concert organisers receive 
for tickets, taking into account Ecco’s 
discounted tickets. The amount of money 
received altogether for tickets is called the 
‘gate’.
c The Three Divas are paid 10% of the 
gate. How much did each of them 
receive? 
3

T-shirts, CDs and DVDs were sold at interval and at the end of the show. T-shirts were sold 
for $17.50 each, CDs for $20 each and DVDs for $25 each. GLAM Events recorded 5200 
people attending the event!
a If 40% of attendees bought T-shirts, calculate the amount of money made in sales from 
this product. 
b If 45% of attendees bought CDs, calculate the amount of money made in sales from 
this product.
c If 60% of those who bought CDs also bought DVDs, calculate the amount of money 
made in sales from DVDs.
d Calculate the average amount per attendee that GLAM received from merchandise sales.
I saw, I volleyed and I bought the t-Shirt! 
Over a 10-day tennis tournament, WonderDome Australia sets up booths selling event-related 
merchandise. The organisers arrange to sell T-Shirts, caps, tournament rackets and a pack of 
four tennis balls. All products bear the Golden Racquet Tournament logo. 
managing event merchandise

a picture speaks volumes!

8.9-cm square picture frame. The frame is designed to fit a 
photo measuring 4.1 cm by 5 cm at its centre. 
a Find the area of:
 i the picture frame  
ii   the photo  
iii   the part not covered by the photo.

extra 20 to cover breakages. The cost of the photos is $2.50 each and the frames will 
cost $3.76 each. 
 i Christian and Evol received a 15% discount on the cost of the photos because they 
ordered so many of them. How much did they pay for all the photos?
 ii Calculate the cost to Christian and Evol for all the complete frame and photo sets.

Did you get me a catalogue?

are equally spread throughout the year but it 
is expected that there will be 20% more visitors 
when the show is on. Calculate how many people could visit the exhibit across all  
4 galleries.
c The catalogue that complements the exhibit retails for $40. Printing cost per catalogue, 
including freight, is $18. Art Industries calculates that 25% of potential patrons will 
purchase a catalogue. Calculate the margin that Art Industries are expecting from the 
sale of all the catalogues.
d Art Industries are donating 5% of the total sales from catalogues to the World 
Agricultural Group. Calculate this figure.

Advertising and promotion are important aspects of event management. The success of an event 
depends on effective communication to the right people, within the right time frame and with the 
right frequency. 
tune-in folks!
1 
Approximately 6.5 million Australians 
tune in to breakfast radio each day across 
5 commercial networks. Of the national

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Conversions – length, time 
1
When you measure quantities such as distance, speed and mass, you need to use different units 
of measurement – depending on which quantity is being measured, and in which country the 
measurements are being made.
In Australia, metric units of measurement are used such as centimetres, metres, kilometres, 
kilometres per hour, grams and kilograms. In the USA, Imperial units of measurement such 
as feet, inches, miles, miles per hour, pounds and ounces are used. In Britain, metric units 
are often used for mass and some lengths, but road distance and road speeds are commonly 
measured in miles and miles per hour.
The size of the quantity you are measuring often  
determines the units to use. For example, the speed of  
a marble rolling along the floor would normally be  
measured in metres per second. Land speed records  
in a car would be measured in kilometres per hour.
So if the speed of a skater is measured in kilometres  
per hour in one place, and in miles per hour in  
another place, how do you compare them?  
The secret is in converting units of measurement,  
so you can make meaningful comparisons.
Converting units of length or distance
The metric system of measurement makes it easy to convert units. It involves either 
multiplying or dividing numbers by tens, hundreds, thousands and so on. For quantities such 
as length and mass, conversions can be made by simply moving the position of the decimal 
point in numbers an appropriate number of places in the correct direction. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
Sprint your way through the following metric conversions.  
Remember:
•  when you are converting from a smaller unit to a bigger unit, the appropriate 
number or factor should be divided 
•  when you are converting from a bigger unit to a smaller unit, the appropriate 
number or factor should be multiplied.
a  1.6 kilometres (km) =                    metres (m)
b 256 millimetres (mm) =                    centimetres (cm) [to 1 decimal place]
c  14 m =                     cm
d 765 m =                    km (to 3 decimal places)
Imperial units of length include inches, feet, yards and miles. 
Conversion between units does not involve multiplying or dividing 
numbers by tens, hundreds or thousands. Some examples are 
shown in the box at the right.
When converting from Imperial units of measurement to  
metric units and vice versa, it is helpful to know the 
conversion factors – that is, the numbers by which you 
multiply or divide to correctly convert the units.  
Some examples are shown in the box at the right.
Imperial units of length
12 inches (in) = 1 foot (ft)
3 feet (ft) = 1 yard (yd)
5280 ft = 1 mile (mi)
1760 yd = 1 mi
1 in = 2.54 cm
1 ft = 30.48 cm
1 ft = 0.31 m
1 mi = 1609.34 m
1 mi = 1.61 km
1 yd = 91.44 cm

Converting units of time
Time is measured by the same units everywhere, and these 
units include seconds, minutes and hours. When comparing 
or converting time units from one to another, it is helpful to 
know the conversion factors which are shown at the right.
4 
Aim for a personal best, as you work through these time conversions:

b 8.45 h =                    min

When converting time, it is important to understand when and how to convert  
decimal components of the units when you are using a combination of  
hours, minutes and seconds in your answer. 
For example:
What is 3.89 hours in hours and minutes?
First convert 0.89 hours to minutes:  
  
0.89 × 60 = 53.4 min
So 3.89 h = 3 h 53.4 min
What is this answer in hours, minutes and seconds?
Convert 0.4 min to seconds:  
  
0.4 × 60 = 24 s
So 3.89 h = 3 h 53 min 24 sec

When you measure quantities such as distance, speed and mass, you need to use different units 
of measurement – depending on which quantity is being measured, and in which country the 
measurements are being made.
In Australia, metric units of measurement are used such as centimetres, metres, kilometres, 
kilometres per hour, grams and kilograms. In the USA, Imperial units of measurement such 
as feet, inches, miles, miles per hour, pounds and ounces are used. In Britain, metric units 
are often used for mass and some lengths, but road distance and road speeds are commonly 
measured in miles and miles per hour.
Converting units of speed
A unit of speed is always shown as a unit of length or distance  
divided by (or ‘per’) a unit of time. Metric units of length or  
distance include centimetres, metres and kilometres; and  
Imperial units include feet, yards and miles. 
It’s time to look at converting units of speed. Let’s  
start with converting kilometres per hour (km/h)  
to miles per hour (mph or mi/h).
For example, the maximum speed limit in  
Australia is 130 km/h on the open highway in  
the Northern Territory. What is this speed in mph?
Converting km to mi: 130 km = 130 ÷ 1.61 = 80.75 mi
In both units of speed, the time unit is the same:  
h (hours).
So 130 km/h = 80.75 mph
1 
Complete the sentences:
a To convert km/h to mph, we                              the km/h figure by 1.61.
b To convert mph to km/h, we                              the mph figure by 1.61.
2 
a 150 km/h =                          mph
b 32 mph =                          km/h
What happens when both the units of distance and the units of time need to be converted?  
Two examples are shown below.
How do we convert 18.6 km/h to m/s?
First convert the unit of length or distance: 
18.6 km = 18 600 m
Then convert the unit of time: 
 
 
1 h = 3 600 s
We now have an equation to solve: 
 
 18 600 m ÷ 3 600 s = 5.17 m/s  
(Rounded to 2 decimal places)
How do we convert 50 mph to m/s?
First convert the unit of length or distance: 
50 mi × 1 609.34 = 80 647
Then convert the unit of time: 
 
 
1 h = 3 600 s 
The equation: 
 
 
 
 
80 647 ÷ 3 600 = 22.40 m/s

Units of measurement of liquid volume also vary between metric and Imperial systems.

Did you know?
People often confuse mass and 
weight, thinking they are the same 
thing. In fact, they are different.
Mass refers to how much matter 
is contained in something. It is 
measured in metric units such as 
grams, kilograms and tons, and 
Imperial units such as ounces and 
pounds.
Weight refers to the force with 
which gravity pulls downwards 
on an object or living thing. It is 
measured in newtons (N), which is 
the unit of measurement for force.
1 lb = 16 oz
1 oz = 28.35 g
1 lb = 453.59 g
1 lb = 0.45 kg

Formula One car racing ranks as one of the world’s fastest, potentially most dangerous, and most 
popular sports. Hundreds of thousands of fans flock to circuits around the globe to watch the events, 
with hundreds of millions more watching on television. Little wonder – these vehicles travel at wild 
speeds. Formula One combines cutting edge racing engineering with the steely skills of the world’s 
top drivers as they push their amazingly quick machines to speeds upwards of 300 km/h.
Formula One racing

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Game fishing is fishing at the serious end! This sport involves fishing for large ocean fish with a mass 
of 400 kg or more. It is popular in many parts of Australia, including along the north coast of 
Queensland. Species of game fish found in that region include Black marlin, Sailfish, Yellow fin tuna, 
Mackerel and Wahoo. Many companies offer fishing charters where groups of people can hire out a 
boat and crew and try their hand at this extreme sport. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
Two couples – Anastasia and Brad, and Omar and Sally – go on a game fishing charter trip 
for a day aboard the vessel The Monster. It leaves Port Douglas in North Queensland at 9 am 
on a Saturday morning.
The Monster is powered by two 440 horsepower (hp) diesel engines. Horsepower is a unit of 
measurement of power used in relation to engines. Its use is not as common now as it once 
was. Today, the most common unit of measurement of power is Watts (W). When measuring 
engine power, 1 hp is approximately equal to 746W. 
1 
What is the maximum power output of The Monster’s two engines in watts?
At sea, distances can be measured in nautical miles (n miles). This unit is different from miles, 
the Imperial unit of measurement for road distances. The speed at which a boat travels across 
the surface of the sea is often measured in knots (kn).  
 
• 1 kn is equal to 1 n mile per hour or 1 n mile/h 
 
• Speed can also be measured in the metric units of kilometres per hour (km/h) 
 
• 1 kn is equivalent to 1.88 km/h
2 
a If a boat is travelling at 19 kn, what is this speed in km/h?
b If a boat is travelling at 64.5 km/h, what is this speed in kn?
Back on our charter, plenty of fishing action went on while the boat was in motion, but The 
Monster also stopped at two different spots during the day where the engines were turned off. 
These spots were both located beyond a number of reefs – just past the Continental Shelf, 
which lies about 55 km off the coast of Port Douglas.

Tag and Release Programmes
Game fishing might bring on an adrenalin rush, but 
there’s a serious side too.
The protection of marine resources is important. 
For many species of fish caught in Australian 
waters, there are regulations about how many fish 
can be taken in one catch, and the minimum mass 
and/or length of fish that can be legally caught and 
kept. With some species, it is illegal to keep any 
fish caught. These regulations aim to ensure that 
different species do not become scarce. 
 
In Australia, tag and release programmes are 
encouraged by fishing associations, government 
departments and environmental groups. They 
involve the insertion of a tag into a caught fish, and 
the release of the fish back into the water. If tagged 
fish are re-caught, details such as location caught 
and length and mass of the fish are recorded.
This data is sent to the agencies that run tag and 
release programmes, and is vitally important in the 
management of marine resources.

So what does it feel like to fly? Skydivers know – jumping out of an aeroplane with a parachute is  
an incredible experience. Imagine the feeling of total freedom as gravity pulls you towards the 
Earth, which – for a short while anyway – seems like a long way down as you plummet towards it 
at 200 km/h! That’s called free-falling. When the parachute opens, the ride downwards becomes a 
lot more controlled and you get to take in views like you’ll see nowhere else – from 1 000 metres or 
more above the Earth.

What’s more extreme than going skydiving yourself, or with friends? Doing it while in the thick  
of fierce competition with other skydivers, that’s what! It all unfolds thousands of metres up in  
the air …
In competitive skydiving, points are awarded to individuals or teams for performance. In 
formation skydiving, teams gain points for performing patterned routines while free falling 
(dropping through the air without their parachutes open). 
The two types of formations are known as randoms and blocks. Randoms involve the team 
making a single formation. Blocks are double formations, with a specific movement pattern 
between them. 
For example, a block formation 
could involve four team members 
linked together in a circle, then 
each team member separates, does 
a 360° turn, and links up in the 
circle again. 
Blocks are worth 1 point for

This is one extreme sport – for participants and spectators alike! V8 Jetsprint racing began in New 
Zealand in the 1980s, and is now also staged in Australia and the USA. It’s sometimes called rally 
driving on water – these boats aren’t that big, but they’re a whole lot more awesome than your 
average rally car. They complete 180 degree corners, pulling a similar magnitude of force to an F-111 
fighter jet, and their acceleration is mind-boggling. Imagine putting a drag racing car’s engine into 
your average aluminium fishing runabout, and you’re close to the mark. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1

acceleration is constant over the 2 seconds, what would be the boat’s speed after:
a 0.5 s?

d 2.0 s? 
e 1.34 s?

Some Jetsprinting boats are powered by engines that produce up to 1 200 horsepower (hp). 
Horsepower is a unit of measurement of power used in relation to engines. Its use is not as 
common now as it once was. Today, the most common unit of measurement for power is 
Watts (W). When measuring engine power, 1 hp is approximately equal to 746W.
4

in Watts?

Jetsprint boats have a typical mass of  
500–600 kg. They have one of the highest  
power-to-weight ratios of any boat, car or  
other vehicle used in motorsports.
a If a Jetsprint boat weighed 600 kg and was powered by an engine with a power output 
of 850 kilowatts (kW), what is the power-to-weight ratio of this vessel? (ratio of kW:kg)
b Why do you think power-to-weight ratio is an important consideration in motorsports?
A Jetsprinting course was constructed over an area roughly equivalent to a football field. The 
channels are between 4 and 8 metres wide, and 1 metre deep. The diagram on the next page 
shows how a typical course might look.
In a race, there are three qualifying rounds where competitors are timed around the course. 
Each boat carries a crew of two – a driver and a navigator. The top 16 then race off in a series 
of ‘sudden death’ rounds, where only the top half of the competitors proceed to the next 
round. The field goes from 16 to 8 to 4 and then the final 2, who race for top spot. The boats 
are required to go around the course, passing the numbered points in a certain sequence. 
A typical race sequence for the course in the diagram might be:

and see how you fare!
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
Women’s surfing sees some amazing waves and amazing rides. Here, we’ve projected into 
the future and summarised the five biggest waves surfed in a competition in 2020.

•  the wave heights were 5.4 m, 6.8 m, 5.2 m, 6.5 m and 5.7 m

perform adrenalin-pumping routines, based on strength, balance and precision timing.

Nothing pumps the adrenalin like white-water rafting. Inflatable boats tumble and belt their way 
through rushing, gushing, swirling rapids – while the rafters inside use their paddles, reflexes, 
judgement and sometimes sheer brute strength to stay on course.
People of any level of experience and expertise can enjoy white-water rafting, although to 
successfully navigate some of Australia’s more rugged stretches of river, rafters should be both 
skilled and experienced.
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
The International White-water River Grading System
To assist rafters in determining the degree  
of difficulty likely to be encountered when 
paddling a white-water river, the International 
White-water River Grading System has been 
established. This system grades rivers into one of 
six categories, as you can see in the box at the 
right.

white-water rivers?

for example, an Australian system.

would be most suitable for a  
non-adventurous beginner?
4

recommended for experienced 
rafters?

of rapids that can be experienced 
in the tours run by this company.

waves.
Grade 2 – rapids have regular, medium-sized 
waves and some tactical moves may be 
needed.
Grade 3 – waves of reasonable size; rafters 
likely to need to hold on at times. Technical 
manoeuvring of raft required to negotiate 
rapids.
Grade 4 – difficult rapids with high powered 
and irregular waves. Continual manoeuvring 
of raft required to negotiate rapids.
Grade 5 – very difficult rapids with large drops 
and fast currents. Complex and powerful 
manoeuvring required to negotiate rapids.
Grade 6 – very dangerous rapids; extreme 
technical skill needed to negotiate rapids – 
not attempted by the vast majority of white-
water rafters.

Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
White-water rafting – the costs 
12
As with any extreme sport, appropriate equipment is essential for white-water rafting. Fans of the 
sport usually need to travel some distance to reach the waterways to pursue their sport. One of the 
realities of pursuing most sports or hobbies is their cost. Just as Roula found …
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where 
appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
Roula decided to take up white-water rafting.  
She visited a supplier and priced the basic  
equipment she’d need: 
• Life jacket – $230 
• Paddle – $140 
• Helmet – $90 
• Raft – $1 820 
• Rope – $40 
1 
How much in total would the equipment  
cost Roula?
2 
Correct to 1 decimal place, what percentage  
of the total bill is represented by:
a the raft? 
b the life jacket? 
c the helmet?
3 
Roula found out that if she purchased all five pieces of equipment online, she would 
receive a 15 per cent discount.
a How much would she save off the total price by purchasing online?
b If she purchased online, how much in total would she spend?
4 
Roula also found that she could hire a raft at a cost of $125 for a weekend. All the other 
equipment she needs could be hired for a further $80 per weekend. She planned to go 
rafting on 12 weekends in a year. 
 
Over the course of a year, would it be more or less expensive to hire the equipment rather 
than purchase it? 
5 
The supplier told Roula that if she purchased the raft for $1 820 and it was in good 
condition after one year, they would buy it back from her for 45 per cent of the purchase 
price and use it as a hire raft.
a If Roula did this, how much would the supplier pay her for the raft after 12 months?
b How much would the raft have cost her for the 12 months if she sold it back to the 
supplier?
c How many times would the supplier have to hire the raft out before they had recovered 
the money paid to Roula for the used raft?
6 
When looking at different rafts, Roula found that the dimensions of different models 
varied. One raft she saw measured 4.2 m long and 2.1 m wide. Another one was 5.5 m 
long and 2.4 m wide. These are the measurements of deflated rafts.
 
What is the total area occupied by each type of raft when deflated?
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 014 4	     Maths in Extreme Sport

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
27
7 
There are two white-water rafting locations that Roula is keen to visit. One is close enough 
to her home to visit in a day, but the other is further and requires a weekend. 
 
Roula calculated that the cost of fuel and provisions for the day trip would be $160 each 
time, and the cost for fuel and provisions for a weekend trip would be $280. 
 
If she purchased all her equipment at the online price calculated in question 3, and over 
the course of a year visited each of the two locations six times, how much would her 
rafting cost her for one year?
8 
Using your answer to question 7, calculate Roula’s costs per rafting trip over the course  
of one year.
9 
Over the summer holidays, Roula and three friends – Bronwyn, Callum and Ahmed – 
decide to go interstate on a rafting holiday. 
•  Roula has her raft and other equipment, but they need to hire another raft at a cost of 
$330 for 10 days and three sets of equipment for $120 each for 10 nights. 
•  They calculate that fuel and other vehicle expenses for the holiday will cost $600, and 
they also need to hire a trailer to carry their equipment at a cost of $200. 
•  Entry to the National Park they plan to visit is $50, and camping fees are $12 per 
person per night. 
•  They have budgeted $720 between them for food and other provisions for the holiday.
 
What is the total cost for the four of them to take the holiday? 
10 The hire fees for the raft and equipment  
are being shared by Roula’s three friends.  
All other costs are being  
divided equally between  
the four of them.

out how much it costs each  
person for the holiday.

money was spent in each category listed in the left hand column. The pictogram needs to 
show only the total money spent on each category, not how much each person spent.
 
Use different symbols for each category, and choose symbols that each relate in some way
