28 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
And now for something completely different! Sphereing or Zorbing (also sometimes called  
Globe-riding) involves participants travelling inside a sphere which is usually constructed of 
transparent, flexible plastic. 
There is one sphere inside another sphere, with an  
air layer in between to act as a shock absorber.  
The inner and outer spheres are often joined by  
dozens of ropes. A person enters the inner  
sphere through a porthole.
The name ‘zorbing’ originates with three New  
Zealand business partners. They conceived  
the idea for a sphere, called it the ‘zorb’, and  
patented it and trademarked the name in  
1994. They created the company Zorb Ltd,  
and set about franchising the business model.
Sphereing is generally done just for fun,  
not competition. The sphere usually moves  
down a gentle slope so the rider rolls downhill,  
but it is also possible to travel on a level  
surface or on water. 
Most spheres are constructed for a single rider, but some hold two or three. The length of 
sphereing runs can be up to 0.81 km (0.5 mi), and they typically reach speeds of 32–48 km/h 
(20–30 mph).
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
In 2006, the Guinness Book of Records officially recognised two world sphereing records – 
the longest continuous distance travelled, and the fastest speed.
 
Both records were made at the Matarua Farm near Rotorua in New Zealand. Steve Camp 
rolled the longest continuous distance of 570 m, and Keith Kolvers set a world zorb speed 
record of 52 km/h (32 mph).
a In the 2008 Beijing Olympics, Jamaican sprint champion Usain Bolt set a new world 
record for the 100 m sprint. He ran it in 9.69 seconds. Which speed was faster – Bolt’s 
run at Beijing, or Kolvers’ speed inside the sphere?
b The longest recorded golf drive in the world was hit in 1974 by Mike Austin at the 
National Seniors Open in 1974. Assisted by a 30 mph wind, Austin drove the tee shot a 
massive 1 545 feet. Was this a longer or shorter distance than Steve Camp’s continuous 
roll in a sphere? By how much?
2 
Some spheres contain a harness, which holds the participant in a relatively fixed position 
inside. Others allow participants to move freely within the sphere. If a person was 
strapped into a harness inside a sphere which rolled 100 m, and the sphere completed 
one complete rotation every 12.98 m, through how many degrees would the person rotate 
in that 100 m roll?
3 
Spheres typically have a diameter of around 3 m.
a Define diameter.
b If a sphere has a diameter of 3 m, what is its radius?
Sphereing or zorbing? 
13
© Blake Education   978 1 92571 014 4	     Maths in Extreme Sport

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
29
A number of different quantities of circles and spheres can be calculated using formulae. 
These include the following.
•  The circumference of a circle = 2 π r. Assume π = 3.14.
•  The surface area of a sphere = 4 π r 2  
Area is measured in units of length squared; e.g. m2 or cm2.
•  The volume of a sphere = 4 
3π r 3  
   Volume is measured in units of length cubed;  
   e.g. m3 or cm3.
4 
a Define circumference.
b Define surface area of a sphere.
c Define volume of a sphere.
5 
On a sphereing run in Queensland, the spheres in use have an outer diameter of 2.91 m.
a What is the radius of the outer spheres?
b What is the circumference of the outer spheres?
c If the circumference of the inner sphere is 6.15 m, what is the diameter of the  
inner sphere?
d If a person of height 173 cm was standing inside the inner sphere, how much space 
would there be between the top of the person’s head and the surface of the sphere?
6 
Calculate the surface area: 
a for the outer sphere described in question 5.
b for the inner sphere described in question 5. 
 
Remember, the units are squared!
7 
Using the dimensions given for the spheres in question 5, calculate the volume of air  
held between the outer sphere and the inner sphere. Remember, the units are cubed!
a To do this, you will need to complete a three-stage calculation. First list the three stages.
b Now, perform those calculations!
8 
In question 5, you calculated the radius of the outer sphere  
and the diameter of the inner sphere.
a What is the radius of the inner sphere?
b Calculate the total volume of the outer sphere. 
c Calculate the volume of the inner sphere.
d Calculate the volume of air held between the outer and inner spheres.
9 
A standard men’s basketball has a diameter of 23.8 cm.  
a Calculate the volume of this basketball.
b Using your answer to question 8b, how many basketballs would fit inside  
a sphere with the dimensions given in question 5?
 Sphereing or zorbing? (cont’d)

30 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Skateboarding – pastime, means of transportation, and extreme sport! Today, mind-blowing speeds 
and tricks on skateboards have reached levels that were not even dreamed of just a couple of 
decades ago. As with any extreme sport, there are always those who want to push the boundaries 
that little bit further …
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
Danny Way from California, a renowned extreme skater, 
holds a number of records. In 2004, he set the world record 
for the longest jump and the highest air off a ‘Mega Ramp’ he 
designed. The jump measured an impressive 79 feet in length, 
and 23.5 feet in height. The same style of ‘Mega Ramp’ was 
used in Way’s successful jump over the Great Wall of China 
in 2005, where he became the first human to jump the wall 
without the aid of a motor.
a How long and high were Danny Way’s jump records, in metres?
b Danny reached an amazing speed of 55 mph before leaving the 
ramp. Read ‘Did you know?’ box about Joel King’s record on a  
jet-powered skateboard. 
 What percentage of Joel King’s speed did 
Danny Way achieve without a motor?
c If speed on leaving the ramp is the 
only factor in determining the height 
and length of a skateboard jump, what 
height and length of jump would be 
achieved by exiting the ramp at the 
same speed Joel King travelled on his  
jet-powered board? Answer in feet, and 
then convert your answer to metres.
d Speed on exiting the ramp is clearly not 
the only factor that determines how long 
and high a jump is. What other factors 
do you think might influence the jump?
2 
Chad Fernandez, an American 
professional skateboarder, performed the 
longest skateboard rail grind – 10.31 m  
(36 ft 9 in or 36.75 ft). If the rail length was 15.00 m in total,  
what proportion of the rail was covered by Fernandez’s grind?
3 
Using your answer to question 2:
a what is this figure as a fraction in its simplest form?
b what is this figure as a percentage?
4 
Another skateboarder competing in the grind-off  
with Fernandez achieved a grind length of 8.99 m.  
How far short of Fernandez’s record was this grind?
5 
World rail-grinding records on skateboards are considerably  
shorter than those set on snowboards and skis. Identify one main difference  
between grinding on skateboards and skis/snowboards that accounts for this.
Skateboarding – jump, grind & slalom  
14
Did you know? 
On 29 August 2007, Englishman Joel King 
clocked up an astounding 110 mph  
(177.1 km/h) on a jet-powered skateboard 
… Now that’s extreme! He laid down on his 
back on the 1.5 m long board, which had a 
kerosene engine strapped to the back. It took 
him just over 2 seconds to reach the record 
speed. The board, which was constructed 
without any steering mechanism or brakes and 
cost King £7 000 (about $16 000) to build.
American Gary Hardwick clocked 63 miles 
per hour – about 101 km/h – on a skateboard 
without any help from engines.
Biker Sherlock holds the record for the fastest 
speed while being towed by a motorcycle –  
90 mph, or 145 km/h …Insane!
Imperial units of length
12 inches (in) = 1 foot (ft)
3 feet (ft) = 1 yard (yd)
5 280 ft = 1 mile (mi)
1 760 yd = 1 mi
1 in = 2.54 cm
1 ft = 30.48 cm
1 ft = 0.31 m
1 mi = 1 609.34 m

Slalom competition in skateboarding involves placing a course of cones along a road, and 
the skaters weave between them. Slalom courses vary in length, but typically consist of 40, 
60 or even 100 cones – placed 2 m (about 6 ft) apart. Competitors are judged by the time 
they clock for the course, and how many cones are touched or knocked over on the way. 
 
The record for slalom skateboarding around 100 cones placed 6 ft apart was set by  
Martin Sweeney of the UK in 1991. Sweeney did the course in an incredible 21.7 s – 
without knocking over a single cone. The previous world record for the same slalom 
course was 25.27 s. 
a How much time did Martin Sweeney shave off the world record?
b What percentage did he take off the previous record?
c On average, how often did Martin Sweeney skate past a cone on his record-breaking 
slalom run?

Use colour coding to show the times for all three slalom courses (40, 60 and 100 cones) 
in a single column for each competitor. Make sure you include the key for the colour 
coding on your graph.
The Ollie
The ollie is a skateboarding trick invented by Alan ‘Ollie’ Gelfand in 1976, and this trick 
transformed the sport. It is an aerial manoeuvre which forms the basis of many other 
skateboarding tricks, such as the kick-flip, the heel-flip and the pop-shoveit. The ollie involves 
becoming airborne on a skateboard without holding the board. Danny Wainwright from 
England holds the official record for the highest ollie at 44.5 inches (113 cm).

Whether it’s at elite level or street level, skateboards take a fair bit of punishment. It’s critical for 
a skater’s equipment to be built to take what’s dished out to it. Let’s look at the bits and pieces that 
make up a skateboard, and some of the specifications that go along with them.
There are four main components to a skateboard:
• the deck
•  the trucks (the axle that connects  
to the underneath of the deck)
• the wheels
• the bearings (inside the wheels).
So whether you’re putting together your own skateboard from the components, or purchasing 
one complete – how do you decide what’s right for you? 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.

In the case of a cylindrical skateboard wheel, height can be taken

The width of skateboard decks does not vary a 
great deal. Most are 7.5–8 inches wide (19.05–
20.32 cm). The size of the skateboarder’s feet 
is also a consideration – people with larger feet 
should use wider skateboard decks.
The Trucks
There are a range of different trucks available 
of varying quality, width and design. 
Essentially, trucks need to match the width of 
a skateboard deck, and be strong and flexible 
enough to do what a skateboarder wants his or 
her board to do.
The Wheels
There are many different types of wheels.  
They are constructed differently – using 
different materials – and come in a range of 
diameters. The two main measurements to 
consider for skateboard wheels are wheel 
diameter and hardness.
The hardness of wheels varies according to the 
types of surfaces they will be ridden on, and 
is given by a number. The higher the number, 
the harder the wheel. Typically, skateboard 
wheels have a diameter of 52–54 mm, with a 
hardness of 95–100a. Cruising skateboarders 
often prefer softer wheels, as they traverse 
rough terrain more often. Typical hardness of 
these wheels might be 75–85a.

Luge is a winter sport where competitors lie on their backs on an amazingly fast, sled-like vehicle 
and fly down a twisting ice-covered course – typically between 1 000 and 1 500 km in length. 
They can reach speeds in excess of 130 km/h. Competitors are timed over a number of runs, and the 
person with the fastest combined times wins the competition. Luge competition is held in women’s 
and men’s singles and doubles and mixed doubles.
‘Luge’ is the French word for ‘sled’. The luges used in elite  
competition, including the Winter Olympics, consist of a  
fibreglass shell with steel runners that slide over the surface of  
the ice. A luge can be steered, but it has no brakes. Once the luge  
is in motion, the competitor lies down and completes the course.  
To stop it, they sit up and pull the front of the luge upwards.
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate,  
unless indicated otherwise.
1 
In a recent international luge competition in Finland, the length  
of the course for men was 1 463 m. The women’s course was  
917 m in length.
a What was the length of the men’s course in kilometres?
b What was the length of the women’s course in kilometres?
c How much longer than the women’s course was the men’s course?  
Answer in metres, then convert your answer to kilometres.
2 
Luge courses are constructed to run downhill, which maximises  
possible speed during competitions. On the course described in  
question 1, the total vertical drop from the start of the women’s  
course to the finish was 58.91 m. For the men’s course,  
the vertical drop was 113.48 m.
 
On two separate graphs, show the gradient (slope) of  
each course. Put length of the course on the x-axis  
(horizontal axis) and vertical drop on the y-axis  
(vertical axis). Set up a suitable scale on the axes of each graph.  
On your vertical scale, make the height at the finish of the course 0 m.

by expressing the ratio of the vertical drop to the length of the course as a percentage.  
To calculate this percentage, divide the vertical drop by the length of the course and 
multiply by 100. What is the grade of:
a the women’s course?  
b the men’s course?

Stunt flying is where pilots in a huge range of different planes – from 70 year-old  
biplanes to modern supersonic jets – perform many different acrobatics in the air. 
It is one of the most dangerous and spectacular extreme sports. Pilots must be highly skilled,  
steady and sure enough to fly at high speeds performing acrobatics and formation flying with 
absolute precision. They must also enjoy showing off their awesome skills in front of big crowds.  
Air shows around the world attract millions of people each year, and stunt flying teams are often  
a part of major sporting and cultural events.

a 75 km/h. 
b 115 km/h.
c 140 km/h.

Faster, higher, pushing boundaries further … Extreme athletes are highly skilled, a bit crazy and very 
out there. All over the world, extreme sports fanatics are smashing records!
Test your extreme sports knowledge on a few random facts and figures that illustrate some of the 
awesome, death-defying and downright dangerous stuff that people get up to.
While your answers to many of these questions are likely to come down to best estimates, 
think about the human feats being performed and base your estimates on a reasonable 
understanding of what might be possible when someone takes an extreme approach to their 
sport! You could run a competition in groups, or you might just like to discuss the answers 
with others. We don’t promise there won’t be clashes of opinion, but we can at least settle any 
arguments.

44 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009
Faster, higher, pushing boundaries further … These extreme sports freaks are addicted to travelling 
fast – hitting breakneck speeds on road, rail and in the air. Exercise your extreme calculation skills 
by crunching the numbers involved in these speed records. 
Round all your answers to 2 decimal places where appropriate, unless indicated otherwise.
1 
The land speed record in a vehicle is held by Andy Green, who went an amazing  
1 228 km/h in 1997 in his ‘ThrustSSC’ vehicle powered by two massive jet engines.  
This is just 7 km/h less than the speed of sound.
a Convert 1 228 km/h to miles per hour (mph).
b Convert this speed to metres per second (m/s).
c What is the speed of sound in m/s?
2 
The motorcycle land speed record is currently held by Chris Carr, who clocked an 
awesome speed equivalent to 158.11 m/s.
a Convert this speed to km/h.
b Convert this speed to mph.
The land speed record – maintained for at least 1 km – was first measured in 1898 at a 
frightening 63.15 km/h. This record was broken many times during the 1900s. Here’s a 
snapshot of some of the landmark records:
• In 1899, the record stood at a hair-raising 105.88 km/h.
• By 1906, this had increased by nearly 100 km/h to an astonishing 205.44 km/h.
• The 400 km/h mark was exceeded for the first time in 1932, when the somewhat more 
serious speed of 404.49 km/h was achieved.
• Just 15 years later, the record had cracked the 600 km/h mark – 633.79 km/h in 1947.
• In 1970, the 1 000 km/h barrier was broken, with the record set at 1 014.52 km/h. The 
record of 1 228 km/h set in 1997 has stood for 11 years, and was the current record at 
the time of printing this book.
3 
a By what factor did the land speed record increase from the previous record in each of 
the years 1906, 1932, 1947, 1970 and 1997? 
b Between which years of those given above did the speeds proportionally increase the 
most? 
c Between which years did the speed increase the most in km/h?
4 
Construct a column 
graph to represent 
the land speed record 
information. Put each 
year along the x-axis 
(horizontal axis) and 
speed along the y-axis 
(vertical axis).

1 mile = 1 609.34 metres

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Extreme Sports 
45
5 
Not quite sport, but a sporting connection … In the build-up to the Beijing Olympics in 
2008, China set a new world record – it put into service the Beijing-Tianjin Intercity Rail. 
This high speed train became the fastest commercially operating rail service in the world. 
At the maximum operating speed on this train, it would be possible to travel 87.5 km in 
just 15 minutes.
a What is the train’s maximum speed in km/h?
b How far would the train travel in 10 minutes at maximum speed?
c In travelling time, how long would it take to journey 500 km at this speed?
6 
On the subject of fast trains, a number of non-commercially operating trains on rails 
have achieved speeds faster than the Chinese Intercity train. In fact, the highest speed 
ever recorded by a ‘train’ – in this case a railed vehicle associated with the testing of US 
army rocket-propelled missiles – is 10 400 km/h.
a Convert this speed to m/s.
b How many km/s is this?
c If a track for a railed vehicle capable of travelling at this speed was built from the east 
coast across Australia to the west coast – approximately 4 000 km – how long would it 
take the rocket-propelled vehicle to travel from one side of the country to another if it 
could maintain this speed?
d If the vehicle kept travelling at this speed from one side of the country to the other for  
2 h 17 min – how many kilometres would it have travelled?
Slowing down a pace now, but still at the extreme end of sports action – hot air ballooning!
•   American adventurer and businessman, Steve Fossett,  
was well known for pushing the boundaries. In 2002,  
he became the first person to circumnavigate the  
world non-stop in a hot air balloon. His balloon was  
10 storeys high and was named ‘The Spirit of Freedom’.  
He made the trip solo. 
•   He took off from Northam in Western Australia on  
19 June 2002 and returned to land in Queensland on  
3 July 2002. The flight took him 13 days, 8 hours and  
33 minutes. He covered a distance of 20 626.48 miles.
•   Fossett’s top speed during the flight was 186 mph over  
the Indian Ocean, and he set a new record for the  
longest distance flown in a balloon over 24 hours –  
3 186.8 miles on 1 July 2002.
•   Steve Fossett went missing in October 2007 after failing to return from flying his plane 
over the Nevada Desert in the USA. A year later, the wreckage of his plane was found.
7 
a For how many hours in total was Fossett flying on his circumnavigation of the Earth?
b What was Steve Fossett’s average speed in mph during the circumnavigation?
c Convert the total distance flown to km and the average speed to km/h.
d Convert the maximum speed during the circumnavigation to km/h.
e If Steve Fossett had flown at his average speed constantly for the entire flight, how far 
(in km and in miles) would he have flown after:
 – reaching the halfway point? 
 
– one week?

probably use Mathematics more than most people because the role involves watching sales, 
developing ranges, negotiating costs and deliveries, and researching the market. Other parts of 
the fashion industry can involve packing slips, delivery dockets, requisition, quality control, stock 
management and bills of lading, all of which require mathematical skills. 
Items of clothing and footwear

8 
Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Fashion is a global phenomenon. While certainly there are some countries where clothing, footwear, 
textiles and leather are just part of everyday life, style and the design of fashion is an industry that 
continues to play a large part in world trade and employment opportunities.
1 
‘You gotta look cool while you’re skateboarding 
and it can cost quite a bit,’ said Mike. He has 
already bought a pair of new skater high top 
Reverse kicks for $124.95, a black CD sweatshirt 
with dark brown detailing for $39.50 and Hevi 
Grouse jeans for $149.99. His Flexifit cap was $25 
and the black bandana $9.99. Of course, the most 
important accessory for a boarder is sunglasses 
and he is showing off his black-tinted Demon 
sunglasses that he got on sale for $50, originally 
$149.99. 
 
When he gets enough money he wants to buy the 
wallet and back pack which will cost him a total 
of $57.95. How much will it cost altogether for 
Mike to be ‘skater chic’?
2 
According to the Organic Trade Association, textile fibre sales are the third fastest growing 
category of all non-food organic products, with sales of $160 million in 2005. This 
increased from $85 million in 2003. What has been the percentage increase in sales in 
that period? Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
3 
The US Government indicated that in 2004 approximately 17 000 people worked as 
fashion designers. Of these, 25% were self-employed, 25% were clothing wholesalers and 
15% were clothing manufacturers. 
a How many designers were:
i self-employed? 
ii clothing wholesalers? 
iii   clothing manufacturers?
b If the rest of the fashion designers were in management positions, how many were in 
management?
4 
According to government records, consumers spent a record $350 billion on apparel and 
footwear in a particular country last year. This was an average of $1 800 for each woman, 
man and child.
a How many people lived in that country according to this data? (Hint: one billion is a 
thousand million.) Answer correct to the nearest whole number.
b These sales from clothing and footwear stores were 6.1% higher than in the previous 
year. How much did consumers spend in total in the previous year? Answer to the 
nearest billion dollars.
5 
The number of fashion designers working in Australia in the years 1991, 2001 and 2006 
was counted and found to be 2 054, 2 575 and 2 700 respectively. The data for 1996 was 
lost, but it is known that the figures for 1991, 1996, 2001 and 2006 average 2 498.75.  
How many fashion designers were working in Australia in 1996?

12 
Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
The patterns and shapes in textile designs vary between cultures. For example, there are the Maori 
diagonals, Hmong spirals, Mayan spiny stars, Navajo eye-dazzlers and Amish four-patch designs.  
Some patterns have special symmetry.  Many are made by repeating shapes over and over again to 
cover a space without leaving any gaps or having any overlaps. These are called tessellations. Often 
traditional designs play a significant role in the development of modern fashions.
Maori diagonals
1 
The diagonal pattern started below is to cover the whole 
140 cm by 80 cm panel.
a Complete the pattern for the whole panel.
b Find the total area of grey squares on the panel.
c Find the area of the panel not covered by grey squares.
d A new panel is to be made 
with the same width of  
80 cm but a different length.  
How long will the panel be if 
the basic pattern repeats  
6 times?
tessellations and tiling patterns
2

a 10 squares 
    b   18 triangles

The patterns and shapes in textile designs vary between cultures. For example, there are the Maori 
diagonals, Hmong spirals, Mayan spiny stars, Navajo eye-dazzlers and Amish four-patch designs.  
Some patterns have special symmetry.  Many are made by repeating shapes over and over again to 
cover a space without leaving any gaps or having any overlaps. These are called tessellations. Often 
traditional designs play a significant role in the development of modern fashions.
navajo eye dazzlers
1 
At an auction of ‘eye-dazzler’ weavings, these 
items were sold: 8 pillow covers measuring  
60 cm2 for $280 each, a 43 cm2 woven picture  
for $550 and a sampler measuring 40 cm by  
54 cm for $350. A blanket measuring 270 cm  
by 210 cm was very expensive at $15 500.  
a How much was paid in total for the Navajo 
weavings?
b Which was the most expensive weaving in cents per square centimetre?
2 
The auctioneer said: ‘The price of such weavings has risen between 10 and 40% in less 
than two years. During the last decade (10 years), they have increased 10 times or more 
in value.’ To the nearest whole number, how much would one of the pillow covers have 
been worth: 
a 2 years ago?  
b 10 years ago?
hmong spirals
A spiral is a curve in the plane that runs around a centre. There are many types of spirals. The 
easiest way to draw them is to plot points on special graph paper called polar graph paper. 
Each point is marked according to its radius from the centre (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5) and its angle 
around the centre (0°, 30°, 60°, 90°, … , 360°).
3

• [3, 60°] 
• [1, 150°]
• [4, 210°]  
• [2, 330°].

Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
The clothing industry is the second largest industry in the world, after telecommunications. At the 
same time it is the third largest polluter in the world. Tomorrow’s fashions may be made from new 
and exotic materials, may contain bionic devices or be antibacterial. But they will also need to be 
kind to the planet – that is, eco-friendly. Eco-fashion is about making clothes that care for the 
environment, the consumers and the working conditions of the people in the industry.
1 
Handbags made from recycled lolly and chip 
wrappers sell for $28 to $58. It is expected that sales 
of these bags next year will be 1.5 million. What will 
be the value of next year’s sales?
2

kilograms of cotton needed for a T-shirt and a pair of jeans. Answer the following correct 
to 2 decimal places. 
a How many T-shirts and pairs of jeans can be made from 100 kg of cotton? 
b How many kilograms of fertiliser and pesticides are needed to grow 100 kg of cotton?

extremely strong, lightweight, flexible, flame-resistant and five times stronger than steel. 
It is used for protective clothing and bulletproof vests. 
a Find the area of Kevlar fabric needed for a jacket if it is 1.27 m wide and 2 m long.
b Find the weight of the fabric needed for the jacket if 1 m2 of Kevlar fabric weighs 170 g.

Dermasilk is going to be used for socks. The 
sock designers need to know how much sweat 
the average person produces in their feet. 
The average person walks about 10 000 steps 
every day.
a If each step averages 60 centimetres and 
a lifetime of walking averages 65 years

person walk in a lifetime?  
b Earth has a circumference of 40 076 km. 
How many times around the Earth will the 
average person walk in a lifetime? Give 
your answer as a whole number.
c If each of the 125 000 sweat glands in a foot produces

d A pair of cotton socks weighs 45 g and absorbs 10% of its weight in sweat without

i the number of mL of sweat a pair of cotton socks will 
absorb.
ii the number of mL of sweat a pair of Dermasilk socks 
will absorb.
e Use your answer to part c to find if either cotton or 
Dermasilk socks will absorb a day’s sweat.

1 
1 000 000 000 metre.

a How many nanometres thick is graphene?

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Choosing the right size clothing can be rather difficult as you need to know what units of 
measurement and what country’s sizing system are being used. Many designers still use 
inches rather than centimetres and then have to convert the measurements back. Finally, the 
measurement of the actual clothing depends on whether the clothes are designed to be a tight fit or 
a loose fit. Fashion trends usually determine the fit of clothing for a particular season.
Female – What size am I?
1 
The following table shows a sample female size 
chart like those used by designers and retail 
stores in Australia and Asia. European sizes are 
important, as Australian and Asian stores also sell 
European merchandise. Use the table and the fast

in inches. Answer correct to the nearest half inch.
f Sophia is an Italian house model. What is her hip measurements in centimetres?
g Italian swimwear brand Aqua Bella is 
launching a new bikini line at the Milan 
fashion show. Find the bust measurement in 
centimetres of Lola the swimwear house model.

KOOL. In order to attract more customers, they 
have decided to manufacture half sizes from sizes 
6 to 14. This means having a size 7 between size 6 
and size 8, a size 9 between size 8 and size 10 and

be used when developing clothing for 
females and males, including children 
(AS1344-1975). 
•  Australian female sizes were 
established in 1959.
•  Australian female house models are 
usually a standard size 10.
•  European female house models are 
usually a size 40.
•  Lingerie or swimwear house models 
are often size 10 but a size 11 (halfway 
between 10 and 12) in the bust.

20 
Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
A body scanner takes a three-dimensional image of a person from which all the body measurements 
can be found automatically. These measurements can then be sent via the Internet for people to 
make patterns for new clothes or plastic mannequins for displays. Such scans can also help to make 
standard charts of measurements for designers to use. Of course, measurements can vary between 
brands and cultures and often the whole process of design is completed in inches rather than 
centimetres.
Here is Alex’s body scan. Use it to answer the following questions.
1 
How tall is Alex?
2 
How far is it from the top of his 
neck to the top of his head?
3 
How long is his neck?
4 
How far is his knee above the 
floor?
5 
How far is his waist above his belt?
6 
How far is his crotch below his 
buttocks?
7 
If his shirt is to be long enough to 
go from the bottom of his neck to 
his crotch, how long must it be?
8 
The inside leg measurement is 
from the crotch to the bottom of 
the trousers. What is Alex’s  
inside leg measurement?
9 
The girth (circumference) of the 
middle of Alex’s neck is 40.3 cm 
and at the base of his neck it is 
44.9 cm. What is his collar size in 
whole centimetres if he takes the 
average of these two figures?
10 Alex’s chest girth is 109.1 cm and  
his maximum belly circumference 
is 91.5 cm. If he buys a suit:
a what chest size should he buy, 42” or 44”?
b what waist size should he buy, 36” or 38”?

uploads/mathematics/Maths in Fashion/10.title: Getting the colour right
uploads/mathematics/Maths in Fashion/10.subject: Mathematics
uploads/mathematics/Maths in Fashion/10.searchText:
22 
Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
There are three primary colours: red, yellow and blue. These colours can be mixed together to give 
secondary colours: red and yellow make orange, red and blue make purple, and blue and yellow make 
green. Artists use colours in this way. Computers use a system based on red, green and blue. Printing 
uses cyan, magenta, yellow and black.  
It was difficult to describe the approximately 1900 colours available to designers and so the 
Pantone® Matching System was created in 1963. Each of the standard colours is given a number 
such as PMS 194. This number can be used for the fabric, the computer screen or the printed 
brochure without any confusion.
1 
Mauve was the first colour that was not made from insects or plants, and could be  
mass-produced in a factory. In what year did William Perkin accidentally make mauve 
while he was looking for a treatment for malaria? How old was he then? 
 
Hint:  year 
age  = 103 1 
9 and year + age = 1874
2 
So that the designer can see all the colours easily, 
Pantone guides often consist of a number of cardboard 
strips, each printed with related colours. In one 
particular colour guide there are 7 shades per blade. 
How many blades are there in this guide if there are  
1 925 textile colours?
3 
De Milo Designs need 60 different colours for the 
autumn season. To make sure that everyone is working 
with the same colours, they dye 10 cm by 10 cm pieces 
of cotton with each colour. These squares are called ‘swatches’. 
They cut each swatch into 2 cm squares so they can send a 
complete set of the colours to each of their suppliers.
a How many suppliers can be provided with a complete set  
of colours?
b How many 2 cm squares of cotton will they be handling in order to do this?
During the last summer season of 12 weeks, De Milo Swimwear 
sold 1 200 pairs of bathers on the Internet. Each pair cost  
$18.00, and postage and handling of $4.50 per pair was  
added to the price. 
4 
If 12% of those sold were returned because the colour  
was not what the customer expected, how much money  
did De Milo receive for bathers: 
a for the season? 
b per month?
5 
De Milo has been offered software that will make sure that 
the colours the customer sees on the computer screen are 
‘what-you-see-is-what-you-get’. If this software costs $1 500 
per month, is it worth their buying it to make sure that  
there are no returns due to wrong colour?
Getting the colour right 
10
... Fast FashIon FaCts
PMS colours are used in branding 
so that logos and advertising all 
show exactly the same colours.
A country’s flag will have its own 
pantone numbers.
A computer screen does not 
accurately show some colours.
10 cm
2 cm
© Blake Education   ISBN 978 1 92571 010 6	
    Maths in Fashion

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009 
Maths in Fashion 
23
6 
According to research, 60% of Internet shoppers do not trust the colours they see on screen 
and in fact will not buy some items online because of this. They say they would buy if the 
colours were guaranteed to be correct. De Milo Swimwear does guarantee their customers 
will receive the colour they see on the screen. During the next month, of all the people 
who visit the website, 12 500 visits become actual sales.
a How many bathers do De Milo expect to sell?
b How much money will they receive in the month?
c If they paid $25 000 for advertising the guarantee, how much will they receive once this 
cost has been subtracted?
7 
If the PMS colours had been described by 3-digit numbers 
only from 100 to 999, how many colours could have been 
described?
8 
Digital cameras and computers use a different set of 
primary colours: Red, Green and Blue. This is called the 
RGB system. These colours can be mixed together to give 
secondary colours: green and blue make cyan, red and 
blue make magenta, and red and green make yellow. 
a If there are 256 different shades of red, 256 shades of 
green and 256 shades of blue (each going from 0 to 255), 
how many colours are possible under the RGB system? 
b Use the fast fashion facts to find out which colour is  
(0, 0, 0).
c What colour is (255,255,255)?
9 
Most modern colour printing systems use the CMYK 
process, which has four different coloured inks: Cyan, 
Magenta, Yellow and blacK. The UBEAUT team has 
chosen the colours for their new range of scarves:  
PMS 178, 218 and 803.

a What are the names of colours to be used in the scarf range?
b How will these colours be described for the computer screen with the RGB system?
c Look at the format of the CMYK system. How many colours are possible? Give your 
answer as a power of 10.
Getting the colour right (cont’d) 
10
... Fast FashIon FaCts
RGB is called an additive 
system because you start with 
black and add colours. 
A purple colour called 
magenta would have a mix of 
128 parts red, 0 parts green 
and 128 parts blue. 
Another purple has a more 
greenish tone if it is a mix of 
255 parts red, 64 parts green 
and 255 parts blue.
... Fast FashIon FaCts
CMYK is known as a subtractive 
system because you start with 
white and subtract the colours.
Black is needed because cyan, 
magenta and yellow mix to make 
a dirty brown, not a perfect black.

uploads/mathematics/Maths in Fashion/11.subject: Mathematics

24 
Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Australian fashion companies bring textiles, clothing and footwear into Australia from overseas. 
This is called importing. They also sell goods in overseas countries and this is called exporting. Both 
importing and exporting are controlled by laws and can involve paying taxes. It is illegal to import 
fake goods or copies of brand-name items.  
Fashions may be cheaper from overseas
Where you see an ‘idea’ provided for a question, 
complete the calculations in it to find the answer.
1 
a How many counterfeit items of clothing 
are brought into Australia each year? 
 
 Idea: 64 000 000 000 000
b How much do illegal imports of 
clothing cost the local fashion industry 
each year? 
 Idea: $ 102 × 104 × 106 
103
 
2 
What is the difference in millions of dollars between the value of Australian imported 
goods and the value of Australian exported goods?  
Idea: It is a number between 700 and 800 and is only divisible by 2 and 19.
3 
It takes 10 minutes to make a T-shirt. 
a How much does it cost to make a T-shirt if a local worker is paid $8 per hour?
b RIPOFF PTY LTD has moved production of its T-shirts to sweatshop workers overseas, 
who are paid 18 cents per hour. How much does it cost to make a T-shirt there?
c If such a T-shirt is sold for $5, how much profit does RIPOFF make on each T-shirt?
4 
In 2005, sales of clothing, textiles and footwear in New Zealand totalled approximately 
$2.5 billion (thousand million). If Australian products made up 19% of their imported 
clothing and 10% of their imported footwear, how much: 
a was the imported clothing worth? 
b was the imported footwear worth?
5

order.

6 
The import duty on shoes is 10% of the cost. HIQUAL 
imported 500 pairs of shoes at $43.93 per pair.  
a What import duty must HIQUAL pay altogether?
b What is the cost of a pair of shoes, including  
import duty?
c To make a profit of 200%, what should the  
advertised price of a pair of shoes be?
7 
Trudy imported her bridesmaid’s dress from the makers LUVLEE in Vietnam. LUVLEE 
charged Trudy $55.80, including postage. She then had to pay 17.5% import duty. After 
that was added, she had to pay 10% GST (Goods and Services Tax). How much did her 
imported dress cost her in total?
8 
BLING imported 350 pure silk 
sarongs and 120 vintage shawls from 
China. The sarongs were $16 each 
and the duty to be paid was 10%. 
The shawls were two for $60 and the 
duty was 17.5%. Find:
a the total cost of the sarongs, 
including duty.
b the total cost of the shawls, 
including duty.
c the total cost of the order, 
including duty.
9 
When goods arrive from overseas they are inspected by 
customs and a tax must be paid according to a percentage 
of the value of the goods. This tax is called a tariff or 
import duty. The table at the right shows the schedule of 
tariffs on different items of textiles, clothing and footwear.
a USTAR is importing shirts valued at $15.35. How much 
tariff will be charged on each shirt?
b USTAR decides that rather than importing the made-up 
shirt, they will import the fabric for $6.53 per shirt and 
the sewing thread for $0.48 per shirt. How much will the 
tariff be on each shirt then?
c The tariff on clothing is reducing to 10% and all the 
other tariffs are reducing to 5% of the value of goods. 
USTAR needs 500 shirts. 
i How much import duty will they pay for the made-up imported shirts?
ii How much import duty will they pay for the fabric and sewing thread for the shirts?
iii What is the difference in the import duty between importing made-up shirts and just 
the fabric and thread?

Maths in Fashion 
© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Size charts usually give standard measurements for the actual circumference of the body rather 
than the size of the garment. Designers describe the space between your actual body measurements 
and a finished garment as ease. Ease is important in the design process as it results in the 
dimensions we see and how a garment behaves on the body. Ease is also essential for good body 
movement and comfort.
tegan and Josh go shopping

Design lines and silhouettes 
12

•   Ease is the space between the body 
measurement and the finished clothing. It varies 
between clothing styles and between designers.
•   Stretch fabrics require little or no ease. This can 
also be true of knitwear.
•   Silhouettes are the overall outside shape of the 
clothes. They can also be called design lines. 
•   The amount of material and hence the cost 
depends on the shape of the clothes.

b the skirt’s waist size with the relevant ease in inches.

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Ease is the space between the body measurement and the finished garment. A designer adds volume 
to certain types of garments to create the ‘look’ they seek, like in a bridal gown’s full skirt. Ease is 
an important calculation in the making of fashion garments. It’s all a matter of Maths!
body measurements + ease + designer’s ease = actual garment measurments
Tegan and Josh are off to Japan for the holiday season and will go shopping in Tokyo to see the 
famous fashion designs of JOJI-SUN. Walking past the windows of the chic department store PAKU 
in Tokyo Central, they see JOJI-SUN’s awesome clothes. ‘Okay let’s try them on! You first!’
1 
A JOJI-SUN dress is sized S, which is equivalent to an 
Australian size 8, with bust 75 cm and waist 55 cm. It is form 
fitted with an average ease measurement of 7 cm.  
a What is the circumference of the dress at the waist including 
ease? Answer in whole centimetres. 
b Hence use the formula C = 2π r where C is the circumference 
and r is the radius to find the radius of the waist of the dress, 
correct to 2 decimal places. 
c Calculate the dress’s bust measurement, using the given 
ease.
d Hence find the radius of the dress at the bust in centimetres, 
correct to 2 decimal places.
2

the picture. It is marked size M, which is equivalent to a man’s 
32 inch waist. The sarong is worn tight with an ease of ½ inch 
and designer’s ease of 1 inch.  
a What is the total ease used in the sarong?
b Find the measurement of the actual waist of the sarong, 
including eases, correct to 1 decimal place.
c Hence find the radius of the actual waist of the sarong,  
including eases, correct to 1 decimal place.
d The sarong is flared so that the circumference of the hem 
at the bottom is 52 inches. Find the radius of the circle 
formed by the bottom hem.

front which overlaps and measures 15 inches  
at the waist. Calculate the measurement of the  
actual waist of the sarong, including eases and the 
additional wrap panel, correct to 1 decimal place.

30

© Barbara Lynch, Angelo Pantalone and Blake Education 2009
Fashion designers do more than draw pictures (trade sketches) of the clothes they are creating. 
They need to make, or have made, samples for sale and promotion. This means that they need to 
understand what materials to use, how much they will need and how much extra they need to allow 
for sewing garments together. Other items like buttons and zips need to be arranged as well.
1 
Dressmakers traditionally measure 
material by using the fact that 1 metre is 
approximately the distance from an adult’s 
nose to the end of the fingers. Salim needed  
2 metres of material to make a skirt. His nose-
to-finger measurement is actually 103 cm.
a If he used the traditional method to

b How much did he pay for this amount of 
material if it cost $17.50 per metre?
2

1½ times the length of the sleeve. If the dress length is 103 cm and the sleeve length is  
52 cm, how many metres of 115 cm wide material is required to make:
a 1 dress? 
b 5 dresses? 
3 
Each Skippi design skirt for the Japanese market uses 1.3 m of material. Because of the 
pattern on the material, 5% extra will be needed. How much material should be ordered 
altogether to make 500 skirts?
4

shop. The price list is shown at the right. The shop 
recommends that people do not pay more than 5% 
of the value of a dress for alternations. Shiva really 
wants a $350 dress with a multilayered skirt, but it is 
too long and the top side seam and shoulder seams 
need adjusting. Would the shop recommend that 
Shiva have the alterations done?
5 
Material comes in different widths. For the shirt he is 
making, Lee has a choice of using 1.5 m of 150 cm  
wide material costing $19.50 per metre or 2 m of 
110 cm wide material costing $14.50 per metre.  
a Find the cost of the material for the shirt for each width of material.
b Find the area of material in m2 Lee will receive if he chooses: 
i 150 cm wide. 
ii 110 cm wide.
c Find the cost per square metre for each width of material.
d Hence state which material is the cheaper choice.

Everyone involved in the fashion industry, from fashion design studios to retailers, needs to cover 
their costs and to make a profit if they are to stay in business. Money is spent on design and 
making, mark-ups added by wholesalers and margins added by retailers. The companies involved 
could be in different countries and some of the processes could be completed by the same company 
– but still apply the margins and mark-ups! Decisions are made to ensure the best cost, quality and 
scheduling of production to match the market’s needs.

In any one season, designers usually produce a range of clothing with a particular theme for a 
particular target group. For example, in this topic, UDUDE’s target group is people aged 15–20 years 
and the theme is ‘Cowboy Chic’. All the clothing in this collection will have cowboy-like details such 
as Texan emblems, checked patterns for shirts and Laredo boots. 
The designer will also give the designs different names like ‘rancher’ or ‘pancho’ to give them a 
personality within the fashion range and to help sales assistants quickly identify designs in the 
shop. Designers must predict how many products are needed to form the range and in what colours, 
quantities and prices. This is an important part of their job.

The retail selling price of a piece of clothing in a shop is the price you see printed on the swing tag or 
label. This price reflects the cost of designing, making, selling and distributing the item. Of course, 
the shop owner adds a retail margin to cover costs such as rent and wages, as well as their profit.  
In this topic, you will see who makes the money and how much and how a shop adjusts its margins 
across a range of clothes to make the most amount of money! The fashion buyer needs to make 
many of these calculations as a part of the job. They are particularly interested in the return on the 
money invested in designing and making the goods. This is called ROI (return on investment).

If a company is to make a profit, it has to make more money from selling its goods than it spends. 
If it spends more than it earns, then it will make a loss and could eventually go out of business. If 
there is a profit then it can be spent on new products, buying more stock, expanding the business, 
research and development or just put it in the bank. 
In this topic, UDUDE is setting up a table to help keep track of their sales and expenses to make sure 
they continue to make a profit.

make on these sales?

When navigating maps, the mathematics is about direction, scale, 
speed, distance and time. Through the activities below, you’ll explore the 
features of maps and add some essential skills to your mathematics 
mapping toolbox.
Grid references
This street map uses grid references to help you locate  
features such as particular streets or railway stations.

H3. This means that it is located in column H, row 3.

4 
Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
We use electrical energy to power our homes, 
schools and places of work. Generating 
electricity by burning coal or gas in a power 
station is not sustainable, and produces carbon 
dioxide. Using sunlight to make electricity 
is sustainable. A solar panel is a grid of 
photovoltaic cells that convert sunlight  
into electric power. 
Power is measured in watts.  
One kilowatt (kW) = 1000 watts (W). 
A single solar panel produces between  
100 and 200 watts, depending on the brand  
and size. A system of several panels can be 
installed on a house roof to generate some  
or all of the energy used by the household.
1 
How many 100 W panels are needed to produce each amount of electrical power? 
a 1 kW 
b 3 kW
2 
A solar panel system contains ten 200 watt panels.  
What is the total power generated? Answer in kilowatts. 
3 
A 100 W solar panel measures 1670 mm long by 990 mm wide.  
There are 1000 millimetres (mm) in one metre (m).
a What is the area of the panel in square millimetres? 
b Converting to metres, the panel measures               m long by               m wide. 
c What is the panel’s area in square metres?
d How many square millimetres are there in one square metre? 
4 
A solar energy system installed on a school roof is made up of ten 200 W panels,  
each 1.8 m long and 1.1 m wide. The roof is a rectangle 30 m long and 8 m wide.
a What is the area of one solar panel in square metres? 
b What area of the roof is covered by solar panels?
c What is the area of the roof?
d What percentage of the roof area is covered with solar panels?
e How many whole panels will fit across 30 metres of roof if each panel is 1.1 m wide  
and they are laid side-by-side?
f A maximum of four rows of panels can be fitted onto the roof.  
How many panels will that be?

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
Wind is an important source of sustainable 
energy. A wind turbine uses the wind to turn 
its large blades, which drive an electricity 
generator at the top of the tower. Electric 
cables carry the electricity to the  
mains grid. 
Wind farms range from a community 
wind farm with a few turbines, to large 
commercial farms of several hundred 
turbines. 
Wind farms are sited in areas of high wind, 
such as upland ridges and the west coasts 
of Victoria and Tasmania, which lie in the 
‘Roaring Forties’, a high wind zone. 
1 
A typical wind turbine produces about 
20 megawatt hours (MWh) of energy per day.  
On average, a household uses 16 kilowatt hours (kWh) per day 
a One megawatt is the same as 1000 kilowatts.  
How many kilowatts are there in 20 megawatts?
b How many households can a typical wind turbine power?
c How many wind turbines are needed to power a town of 5000 households?
2 
To complete this work sheet, you will need to use the  
trigonometric ratios sine (sin), cosine (cos) and tangent (tan).  
Each ratio involves two sides of a right-angled triangle: 
 
• H (hypotenuse, opposite the right angle) 
 
• O (opposite the angle x) 
 
• A (adjacent or next to the angle x)

b At the same position, Jason measures  
an angle of elevation of 47° to the top of a  
turbine blade as it reaches the top of its rotation. 
i Calculate the height to the top of the blade to the nearest metre. 
ii How long is the blade itself? Answer to the nearest metre.

When waste materials such as manure, 
weeds and food scraps are mixed with water 
and stored in a tank, they decompose and 
produce methane gas. Methane is a biogas 
and a renewable source of fuel. It can be 
used for cooking or to power an electricity 
generator. Rural people in many parts of 
India, Africa and China use small biogas 
generators to provide cooking fuel. Large 
biogas plants are becoming more common 
in Europe, America and Australia.

Timber frame houses used to be built of hardwood from wild 
forests. These days, governments restrict the harvesting of trees 
from public land, to protect what is left. Most building timber 
comes from plantations of fast-growing pine trees. Mature trees 
are felled, the trunks cut into logs between 4 and 6 metres long, 
loaded onto a truck and taken to a mill for cutting into lengths  
of timber. 
The diagram shows the end of a log and the cross sections

The 25 × 100 mm can be used for decking.

16 
Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
A sustainable society is one that recycles or reuses all its 
waste. When it comes to organic waste such as kitchen 
scraps and garden weeds, the best way to recycle these 
materials is to compost them. Anything that has been 
alive can be composted.
1 
A healthy compost heap needs a balance between 
the amount of carbon (brown material) and nitrogen 
(green material). A good balance in a compost 
mixture is a carbon to nitrogen ratio of 30:1. 
a Complete the sentence: 
 The ratio 30:1 means that there should be        times  
as much carbon as nitrogen in a healthy compost heap.
b Dead leaves contain about sixty times as much 
carbon as nitrogen. Write this as a ratio.
2

ratios for some common compost materials.  
The best C:N ratio for compost to rot quickly  
is 30:1.
a Brown materials are those that have a C:N 
ratio of more than 30:1. Name the brown 
materials listed in the table.
b Green materials have C:N ratios of less than 
30:1. List the green materials.
c Complete the sentence: 
 Compost made only of paper and straw will not  
rot quickly because the amount of                is  
too high, compared with the amount of               .

Which material should she add to make a good compost mix: cow manure or straw?
e Which material has more nitrogen per kilogram: food waste or paper?
3 
For many composters, the most important goal is to have roughly equal amounts of green 
and brown materials in their compost heap, either well-mixed or in thin layers.
a Write the ratio of brown to green materials for the following compost heaps,  
in simplest form.
i 15 kg brown to 10 kg green
ii 16 kg brown to 8 kg green
iii 20 kg green to 18 kg brown
iv 2 kg brown to 2.5 kg green
v 2.4 kg brown to 1800 g green
b Which of the compost heaps in part a is likely to produce the best compost?

Usually, some of the material in a compost heap has to be recycled

most sustainable forms of transport are ones that 
do not use fossil fuels such as petrol or gas. These

Travelling by air is the quickest way, and sometimes the only way, 
to reach a destination. Sydney to Melbourne is a one-hour air trip. 
Flights to holiday destinations such as Vietnam or Europe take 
many hours, but the same trip over land and sea takes weeks or 
months. The downside to such quick journeys is the large amount 
of greenhouse gases produced by aeroplanes. Travellers wanting 
to live sustainably can pay a ‘carbon offset’, which helps to fund 
projects that reduce carbon dioxide, such as tree planting.
1 
Trees take carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere and 
store it while they are alive.  
A carbon offset company charges three dollars

d How much will Shahid have to pay at an offset price of $20 per tonne?

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
Water is the most precious commodity  
on the planet. Sustainable water use  
often means using as little as possible,  
especially in dry countries like Australia.
Note: in this work sheet,  
V represents volume in litres;  
t represents time in minutes.
1

beside the correct word statements:  
t > 4, V > 500, V  500, t  4.
a A maximum shower time of 4 minutes
b She wasted over 500 litres
c More than 4 minutes is too long
d They used no more than 500 litres
2 
During a severe drought, a government enforces water restrictions.  
The daily maximum water use per person is 200 litres. At the same time, each person  
is encouraged to use at least 20 litres each day for personal health and hygiene.  
Which of the following inequality expressions is correct in this situation? 
a 20  V  200 
b 20  V  200 
c 20  V  200 
3 
Showering uses a lot of water in the home.  
The Daley family decide to reduce their water use.  
They agree not to use more than 75 litres of water per shower.  
The shower runs at a rate of 15 litres per minute. 
a To find the maximum shower length, solve the inequality 15t  75. 
b To further reduce their water use to no more than 60 litres per shower, the family 
installs a water-saver shower head which runs at 8.5 litres per minute.  
Write a new inequality for the shower length, using t as time in minutes. 
c Solve the inequality from part b to the nearest minute.
4 
Write an inequality to describe each situation.
a The maximum number of minutes (t ) Zak can run a hose to wash his car,  
to avoid using more than 300 litres of water in total.  
The hose delivers water at 20 litres per minute.  
Zak uses an extra 15 litres of hot water in a bucket.
b The minimum number of flushes for the toilet that will  
use a total of more than 200 L per day.  
The toilet uses 12 litres of water per flush.  
In addition, it has a leak which uses 25 litres per day.  
(Use N for number of flushes.)

grown or manufactured. The term ‘food miles’ comes from

grown and made locally have low food miles, so use fewer

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
The clothes we wear are made from raw materials such as  
cotton, wool, hemp, nylon and PET plastic. There are energy  
and environmental costs to growing or making these raw  
materials, and manufacturing the fabric adds an 
extra cost. Most clothing is made in countries 
where wages are low, which adds a human 
cost. Washing clothes uses energy and water, 
and when we’re finished with them, throwing 
clothes away adds an environmental cost. 
When all the costs are added up, our clothes 
cost the planet a lot more than the price we 
pay for them.
1 
Over 50% of clothing is made from cotton. Growing and processing cotton uses  
large amounts of pesticides and bleach. Organic, unbleached cotton is grown  
without pesticides and is more sustainable than non-organic varieties.
 
The Venn diagram represents different  
types of T shirts sold in a store. 
 
Set O represents T shirts made with organic cotton. 
Set L represents T shirts made by workers who are 
paid at least enough money to live on (at least a 
living wage). 
a Match one or more of the four shaded areas  
(A, B, C or D) to each type of T shirts.
i Made from organic cotton and made by workers who are paid at least a living wage.
ii Not made from organic cotton and not made by workers who are paid at least a 
living wage.
iii Made by workers who are paid at least a living wage. 
iv Made from organic cotton.
v Made from organic cotton or made by workers who are paid at least a living wage, 
or both.
b Which T shirts would you expect to be
i most expensive?  
ii     least expensive?
2

shows the percentages of people that always wash a full load, and those that wash  
in cold water.
a Copy the table and calculate the missing percentages.
b Use your completed table to find the following percentages.
i People who always wash a full load  
and use hot water.
ii People who wash a part load and  
use cold water.
iii People who use hot water.
c Which option is 
i least sustainable?   
ii most sustainable?

When the number of people in a community increases, it becomes 
harder for that community to be sustainable. In our modern 
world, human population has been growing exponentially 
for some time. In linear, or straight line growth, the 
same number is added each time period. In 
exponential growth, the number at the start  
of a time period is multiplied by the same 
number each time, to produce the number 
at the start of the next period. This is a 
much more drastic form of growth.
1

Maths in sustainability 
© Christine Henderson and Blake Education 2014
The planet we live on has taken 
a very long time to become a 
place where humans can live. 
We take for granted the fact 
that life forms such as air-
breathing, complex organisms 
like humans can exist on Earth. 
It has not always been so. 
For most of the life of our 
planet, conditions have not 
been suitable for any life forms, 
except in the oceans. 
By looking at the immense time scales involved in the evolution of life on Earth, we can see 
how important it is to live sustainably on the planet to keep conditions right for human 
existence. It’s a long way to the next human-habitable planet.
1 
This work sheet is about working with large numbers written in scientific notation.  
A number written in scientific notation has two parts: a number that is one or more,  
but less than ten, multiplied by a power of ten. 
 
For example, we can write ninety six million as a  
basic numeral 96 000 000, or in scientific notation as 9.6 × 107.  
Four thousand can be written as 4000 (basic numeral) or  
4 × 103 (scientific notation).
a Write forty two million as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
b One billion is one thousand million. Write one billion as 
i a basic numeral   
ii     a number in scientific notation.
c Which of these numbers are correctly written in scientific notation? 
i 2.5 × 104 
 
 
ii     13.6 × 106 
iii 8 × 105  
 
 
iv     0.753 × 108 
2 
Scientists estimate Earth to be four billion, six hundred million years old.
a Write this number as a basic numeral.
b Fill in the gaps to write the age of Earth as a number in scientific notation:   
 4.     × 10     
c Complete the sentence: Earth is four point          billion years old.
d Scientists believe that a collision between Earth and  
a second planet named Theia led to the moon being formed.  
This happened four point five billion, or 4.     × 10    years ago.
e How long after Earth formed did the collision happen? Write the answer   
i in words  
ii     as a basic numeral  
iii     as a number in scientific notation.

Life began to evolve on Earth during the Proterozoic era,  
which lasted from 2420 million years ago to 541 million years ago.
a Write these two numbers in scientific notation.
b How long did the Proterozoic era last? Write your answer 
i as a basic numeral  
ii     in scientific notation.
c Single-cell life forms have been found in rocks that are 1800 million years old.  
How long after the start of the Proterozoic era is this? Answer in scientific notation.
d The first multi-cell life forms appeared one billion years ago.  
How many years is this before the end of the Proterozoic era?  
Answer in scientific notation.
4 
An event called ‘The Great Dying’ occurred at the end of the Permian period (252 million 
years ago). Almost all life on Earth became extinct due to a large rise in CO2 in the 
atmosphere. Massive eruptions of lava in Siberia are thought to have been responsible.
a The eruptions produced 1.5 million cubic kilometres of lava.  
Write this in scientific notation.
b One kilometre = 1000 metres. Volume = length × width × height.  
How many cubic metres are there in one cubic kilometre?  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the volume of lava from part a in cubic metres, in scientific notation.
5 
Butterflies first appeared on Earth 40 million years ago.  
Modern humans evolved 2 hundred thousand years ago.  
How many years before humans did the first butterflies appear? Write your answer 
a as a basic numeral  
b in scientific notation.
6 
There are probably many human-habitable planets like Earth in our galaxy, but a long 
way off. One possibility is a planet that orbits the star Gliese 667C. It might have air and 
water. It is 22 light years from Earth. One light year is the distance travelled by light in 
one year.
a Calculate the number of seconds in one year.  
(3600 seconds = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 365 days = 1 year).  
Answer in scientific notation.
b Light travels at 3 × 105 km per second.  
Use your answer from part a to find how many kilometres there are in a light year.  
Answer in scientific notation.
c Write the distance from Earth to Gliese 667C in kilometres, in scientific notation. 
d Mars is the next planet from the Sun after Earth. When Earth and Mars are closest  
to each other, the distance between them is about 54.6 million kilometres.  
Which option correctly completes the statement?
 The distance from Earth to Gliese 667C is about                times as far as Mars. 
i 38 thousand  
ii     38 million  
iii     38 billion
e If it takes 6 months to get to Mars, how long would it take  
to travel to Gliese 677C at the same average speed?
f Name at least two important differences between Mars and Earth.

A crystal is made up of a set of atoms arranged in an organised way that repeats periodically. It

Time passes

Clocks are used to measure time. Clocks can have a display that is analogue with time indicated 
by the angles between the hands on a dial; or digital as numbers on a 12-hour or 24-hour cycle. A 
portable clock is called a watch, while a highly accurate clock used for technical measurements is 
called a chronometer.

How significant? 
6
Numbers can be expressed correct to a particular number of decimal places or a particular number 
of significant figures. The number of digits we use to describe a measurement is the number of 
significant figures. Numbers with too many decimal places or too many significant figures are  
rounded off.
1	
Count the number of significant figures in each of the following:
a	 23
b	 203
c	 230
d	 23.00

b	 2 significant figures

b	 2 significant figures

 i 2.52

of 2.52 × 109.

a	 Write correct to 2 significant figures:
 i 0.3267
 ii 0.0599
b	 Hence find an approximate value 
of 0.3267 ÷ 0.0599.
Rules for counting significant figures
• Count all zeros within a number as significant 
(2305 and 2.005 have 4 sig figs).
• Count all zeros to the right of the decimal point as 
significant (56.00 and 5.050 have 4 sig figs).
• Don’t count zeros that keep the decimal point in 
place as significant (3200 has only 2 sig figs).  
Rules for Rounding:
Numbers with too many decimal places or 
too many significant figures are rounded off.  
Remember, all digits after the rounding digit 
are dropped. If the digit to the right of the 
rounding digit is equal to or more than 5,  
add 1 to the rounding digit.

Mobile phones 
10
Mobile telephones have now become part of everyday life for many people. This means individuals 
can be contacted 24 hours per day.
1

in the year 2000? 
Idea: 9 million – 107 × 19 × 9 × 4 × 6

the year 2000, 60% of drivers in Western Australia

1 429 723 people of legal driving age who actually 
drive. Approximately how many mobile phones were 
owned by drivers?

27% use their phones at some time during a trip. If there are 5 136 523 drivers in 
Australia, how many could be expected to:
a	 make calls while driving?
b	 use their phones at some time during a trip?
4	
The risk of a learner driver being involved in a fatal car crash is 10 times as much as for 
an experienced driver. This risk is increased by a factor of 4 when the driver is using a 
mobile phone while driving. By what factor is the risk of a learner driver being involved 
in a fatal car crash increased if they are using a mobile phone?
5	
‘Optical zoom’ is like magnifying a picture. So if a picture is magnified six times it is 
usually described as having 6× zoom; the size of the image is six times larger when 
zoomed than when it was not zoomed. The word ‘optical’ just means that it uses the 
camera lens, not a digital system. The camera in Elly’s mobile phone has 12× optical 
zoom but her sister Bea’s has only 8× optical zoom.
a	 What would be the dimensions of the zoomed image of a tree if the unzoomed 
dimensions were 1.5 cm by 0.5 cm:
 i on Elly’s camera?
 ii on Bea’s camera?

to the unzoomed image?

danger. For average drivers, the reaction time is about 1.5 seconds.
a	 If the driver is travelling at 60 km/h at the instant he applies the brakes, how far in 
metres will he travel during that 1.5 seconds?

a mobile phone while driving. What is the reaction time of a driver using a mobile 
phone?

time?

Inventions and patents 
11
When someone invents something new they often protect the idea by ’taking out a patent’. The 
patent describes the invention but stops other people from making or selling it without paying for 
the right.

a	 What percentage of patents was granted?
b	 If each patent application cost approximately $7000, how much money did the patent 
office receive?

Disposable pairs of bamboo chopsticks joined together were invented in Japan in the late 
19th century. Usually they are approximately 25 cm long. If 24 000 000 000 pairs are sold 
each year, how many kilometres of bamboo are needed?

Bicycles 
14
Bicycles are a means of transport as well as being 
ridden as a sport. Tricycles are three-wheeled 
children’s toys.
1	
In the 1970s, Americans bought 11 million 
cars each year. They bought 22% more 
bicycles than cars. How many bicycles did 
they buy?
2	
The cost of a bike in the 1880s was 
approximately $125 at a time when the 
average salary was $450 per year. The 
average salary in Australia is currently  
$54 000. How much would a bike cost now if 
it were the same proportion of average salary?
3	
It has been reported that the number of unhelmeted bike riders in crashes in Florida has 
risen in the years since wearing a helmet was made non-compulsory. In 1999 when it was 
compulsory, 22 unhelmeted riders died. By 2004 the number of fatalities had risen to 250. 
What was the percentage increase in unhelmeted deaths in that time?
4	
Speed records for bicycles have continued to be broken. It was 223.174 km/h in 1973, 
245.08 km/h in 1985 and 268.6 km/h in 1995. What was the percentage increase in 
speed:
a	 between 1973 and 1985?
b	 between 1985 and 1995?

flew 39 metres in 12 seconds at about 3 metres above the ground. How fast did he fly in 
metres per second?
b	 In 1899, ‘Mile-a-Minute Murphy’ set a speed record on his bicycle of 1 mile  
(1.609344 km) in 57.75 seconds. How fast is that in metres per second?
6	
Lilli’s bicycle wheel has a 
circumference of 223 cm. How 
fast was Lilli travelling if her 
wheel made 123 revolutions every 
minute:
a	 in centimetres per minute?
b	 in kilometres per hour?

Bar codes 
16
Bar codes were originally devised to help supermarkets speed up their checkouts. Later it was found 
that they could be linked to inventory and price-control computers. There is some variation in how 
the barcodes are arrived at, depending on the country. These exercises show examples.
1

numbers and a machine-readable barcode.

the last digit is called the ‘check digit’. For this box of tissues:

Work has different meanings depending on the context. It can be a place of employment, a piece of 
fine art or handwork like knitting. Work is done on an object by a force to produce energy, to change

Machines

A machine is anything that moves energy from one place to another or changes it from one form to 
another. So a lever and a pulley, a car and a bicycle are all machines.
1	
A school buys a ‘number equaliser balance’ to teach Arithmetic. Equal weights are hung 
from the numbered rod until it is balanced. In the picture there is one extra weight to be 
hung.
a	 Where should the extra weight be hung so that the number equaliser balances? What 
Arithmetic equation is the balance showing?
b	 Where would the weights need to be hung to show that 5 + 4 = 6 + 3?
c	 How could you show that 10 = 8 + 2?

a	 If the student standing on the end of the 2 m long seesaw weighs 80 kg and the rock is

The simplest machine is a lever comprising a bar and a fulcrum or pivot point. The load 
is put on one end of the bar and you apply your effort at the other end. This allows you to 
move very heavy loads. 
The formula for a simple lever to be balanced is: E × D1 = L × D2
where E is the effort, D1 the length of the bar from the effort to the fulcrum, L the load and 
D2 the length of the bar from the load to the fulcrum. The formula works no matter where 
the fulcrum is.

0.25 hours of brisk walking
6.5 hours of sitting
2 hours of standing
4	
By how much did each contestant’s expended energy exceed, or fall short of, their 
energy intake?
5	
Construct a line graph on graph paper to show the different amounts of energy taken in 
and expended by each of these contestants. Put both lines on the same graph, but use a 
different colour for each one. Make sure you label both lines and the axes clearly, and 
give the graph a title.
Hint: 
Remember the energy 
expended figures 
in the table on the 
previous page are  
kJ burned per kg of 
body weight. 
In your calculations, 
use the contestants’ 
initial weights 
as given at the 
beginning of this 
activity sheet.

14 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
Advertising 
6
Proudly brought to you by a range of calculations involving advertising times, rates, revenue and 
marketing methods.
Billions of dollars are spent every year on television advertising. This money allows 
commercial free-to-air television stations to exist. Many viewers find advertisements irritating, 
but television advertising is a highly effective way for companies, corporations, governments 
and non-profit organisations to get their messages across to the public.
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.
1	
When television advertising is purchased, it is sold in packages, not as single 
advertisements. Different advertising rates are charged according to the city or region in 
which they screen, and the time of day they are shown.
a	 Why do you think advertising rates vary according to the city or region in which they 
are shown?
b	 Why do you think advertising rates vary according to the time of day they are shown?
2	
The basic time unit for advertisements is 30 seconds. Channel 4 charges the following 
rates for advertisements shown between 7 am and 9 am:
•	 In Melbourne – $19 000 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Sydney – $21 500 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Brisbane – $14 200 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Adelaide – $5 200 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
•	 In Perth – $6 700 for 30 × 30-second advertisements
	
Use these rates to calculate how much advertisers pay per advertisement on Channel 4 in 
each city.
3	
An advertiser purchases 30 × 30-second advertising spots to run between 7 am and 9 am 
over the course of two weeks (i.e. Monday to Friday). On average, how many times per 
day would the advertisement be shown?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
15
5	
Prime weekday viewing times are from 6 pm to 9.30 pm. During these times, a 50% 
loading is added to the 7 am to 9 am costs. Between midnight and 7 am, the advertising 
costs are 45% of the 7 am to 9 am costs. 
	
An advertiser wants to run this advertising schedule on Channel 4 in Perth: 
	
J 30 × 30-second advertisements between 7 am and 9 am
	
J 30 × 15-second advertisements between 6 pm and 9.30 pm
	
J 30 × 45-second advertisements between midnight and 7 am
	
What would be the total cost of the campaign?
6	
An advertiser ran 30 × 30-second advertisements on Channel 4 in Adelaide between 7 am 
and 9 am across two weeks. The advertisements offered a special deal on a product, which 
lasted for the length of the advertising campaign. 
	
The deal let viewers purchase the product at 50% of its regular price. The regular price 
was $59. The advertising campaign resulted in 216 sales of the product.
a	 Was the revenue gained from product sales during the advertising campaign more or 
less than the cost of the campaign?
b	 By how much did the revenue gained from the product sales exceed, or fall short of, the 
cost of the campaign?
7	
A movie is scheduled to screen between 8.30 pm and 10.30 pm on a commercial TV 
station. The actual running time of the movie is 108 minutes. However, the station has 
to include 35 × 30-second advertisements and 8 × 15-second station promotions during 
the movie. The movie cannot run past 10.30 pm as the station then crosses live to an 
international tennis tournament.
a	 What length of movie time will need to be cut out to accommodate all the advertising 
and TV station promotions?
b	 What percentage of the total movie time is this?
Advertising (cont’d) 
6
Advertisement length
Cost of 30 ads
Cost of 1 ad
15 seconds
45 seconds
60 seconds
4	
While 30 seconds is the basic time unit for an advertisement, advertisers can purchase  
15-, 45- and 60-second spots too.
•	 15-second advertising spots are charged at 60% of the 30-second rate
•	 45-second advertising spots are charged at 140% of the 30-second rate
•	 60-second advertising spots are charged at 160% of the 30-second rate

between 7 am and 9 am.

proportion, transposing equations and applying formulae.
‘National Icon’ takes young performers and sets them on the road to stardom through a series 
of performances that are scrutinised carefully by a panel of three judges.
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.
