18 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘Out in the Wild’ 
8
The documentary crews are roaming Africa to find out what some of the biggest, cutest and most 
striking animals on the planet are up to. They’ve found some amazing statistics about weights, 
heights and more.
You can travel to the ends of the Earth … and you don’t have to leave home to do it.  
‘Out in the Wild’ brings the world of wildlife to your TV …
1	
The ‘Out in the Wild’ crew visits a region in Tanzania to observe the behaviour of some 
zebra families. Each zebra family has one male (stallion) and 2–6 females (mares), 
together with any young foals. There are also bachelor groups of males that do not have 
families. In the region visited by the crew, the total number of zebras was 216.
a	 151 of the zebras lived in families. What was the total number of male ‘bachelors’?
b	 There were 32 stallions in families. How many families were in the group?
c	 There were a total of 18 foals in the group of zebras. How many adult females were in 
the group?
d	 What was the average number of females per family in the group of zebras? (Answer to 
1 decimal place.)
2	
Further south in Africa, in Botswana, another ‘Out in the Wild’ crew visits a meerkat 
colony with 24 meerkats living together. The total length of an adult meerkat is  
25–31 cm, and their tail length is typically 19–24 cm. They weigh 620–940 g.
a	 In this meerkat colony there are 14 males and 10 females. What is the ratio of males to 
females?
b	 The heaviest male meerkat in the colony is 830 g and the heaviest female is 770 g. 
What proportion of the male’s weight is the female’s weight? (Answer to 2 decimal 
places.)
c	 Four of the juvenile meerkats have a combined tail length of 52 cm. What is their 
average tail length?
d	 One juvenile has a tail 12.4 cm long. When fully grown, her tail will measure 21.2 cm. 
What percentage of the fully-grown tail length is her tail now? (Answer to 1 decimal 
place.)

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
19
3	
One of the most popular segments on ‘Out in the Wild’ was the filming of the birth of a 
baby giraffe in the wild, six years ago.
a	 Female giraffes gestate or carry their young for 457 days. How many months is this? 
(Answer to the nearest whole month.)
b	 When it was born, the young male calf weighed 61 kg and stood 2.01 m high. Six years 
later, the crew revisits the area just south of the Sahara Desert and catches up with the 
same giraffe. Now he is an adult bull weighing 1345 kg and standing 5.67 m high. 
When the calf was born, what percentage of its adult weight and height were its birth 
weight and height? (Answer to 1 decimal place.)
4	
A recent 2-hour special of ‘Out in the Wild’ was filmed at Kruger National 
Park in South Africa. Part of it covered the habits of a population of Southern 
White Rhinoceros. These animals generally move in small groups and are 
quite sociable, although males are very territorial.
a	 Southern White Rhinos behave routinely and have 
favourite places to walk, feed and wallow. Daily 
movements of up to 15 km are not uncommon for 
females. The crew tracked one group of females and 
found that the 4 adults and 1 calf each walked an 
average of 7.8 km per day over the course of a week. 
What was the total distance covered by  
one rhino in a week?
b	 If this rate of movement was 
maintained for a year, what is  
the total distance each rhino  
will have covered?
c	 One bull rhino spent the entire seven days in his home territory, an area of savannah 
totalling 2.37 km2, in the shape shown below. Calculate the value of x, to 2 decimal 
places).

Transforming gardens – the team goes beserk 
on geometric shapes, costing and timing jobs, 
and area calculations.
In the hit TV program ‘Backyard Bonanza’ 
Jack Dare is the star of the show. He and his 
team of garden landscapers, carpenters and

transform the garden over the course of a 
weekend.

for a property they visited recently.
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.

What is the total area of this property?
2	
The team paved the driveway with pavers. What total area was paved?

The top of each paver measured 19 cm × 42 cm. How many were needed to complete the 
driveway? (Round off to the next whole paver.)
4	
Jack can lay 42 pavers in one hour. If his two assistants can keep up with him, how long 
would it take the three of them to pave the entire driveway? (Express your answer in

The pergola has a total of 9 upright support posts, each measuring 2.4 m × 0.1 m × 0.1 m.

The borders around the native grass 
plantation are made from sleepers. To

and aerated, and organic matter was

Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
Here is the News 
10
Breaking stories about sport, natural disasters, traffic, 
crime, the lottery and weather all bring their own set of 
mathematical challenges. Join us after this short break for 
a closer look at percentages, proportions, costs, averages 
and more.
Crime, wars, natural disasters, politics, sport, 
entertainment and weather – news reporters venture 
far and wide to make sure you’re kept informed about 
what’s happening and who it’s happening to.
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to  
2 decimal places.
1	
The police commissioner announced crime figures for the past year. She reported that 
the number of home burglaries had decreased by 439 from last year, with the number of 
reported burglaries this year totaling 4891.
a	 How many burglaries were reported last year?
b	 By what percentage had the number of burglaries decreased? Answer correct to  
1 decimal place.
2	
Traffic came to a standstill in the city today when a truck carrying a load of bananas 
overturned. Fortunately no one was injured, but two-fifths of a tonne of bananas were 
ruined. If bananas retail at $8.99 a kilogram, what is the value of the bananas that 
were ruined?
3	
The Prime Minister said funding would be made available this year to extend Highway 1 
by 34 kilometres. The total funding required is $182 million.
a	 What is the cost per kilometre of new road?
b	 At this rate, how much would it cost to extend the highway a total of 51 kilometres?
4	
The city zoo took delivery of its newest attraction: a three-year-old  
male giraffe. It was transported by ship to the port and then by a  
specially prepared truck to the zoo. The giraffe weighs 1.64 tonnes  
and stands 3.68 metres high. It joins four others at the zoo.
a	 How many kilograms does the giraffe weigh?
b	 If the combined weight of the zoo’s five giraffes is  
5.87 tonnes, what is the average weight of each  
one in kilograms?
c	 How many centimetres high is the giraffe?
	
The giraffe is not the heaviest animal at the zoo.  
One of the elephants weighs 4010 kilograms.
d	 What is the elephant’s weight in tonnes?
e	 In tonnes, how much heavier is the  
elephant than the giraffe?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
23
Here is the News (cont’d) 
10
5	
The Rockets re-signed their star 
defender today in a deal believed to be 
worth a total of $1.6 million over five 
years. The contract is structured so he 
will be paid 0.12 of his fee in the first 
year, 0.13 in the second year, and 0.22 
in the third and fourth years.
a	 What proportion of the total fee does 
he get paid in the fifth year?
b	 Calculate how much money he gets 
paid in each of the five years of his 
contract.
6	
Overseas, and an earthquake has struck an isolated part of Turkey. Scientists report it 
measured 6.0 on the Richter scale. The Richter scale is a logarithmic scale that measures 
the size (amplitude) of the shockwave resulting from an earthquake. Each whole number 
increase in the Richter scale means the size of the shockwave increases ten times.
a	 How much bigger are the shockwaves of this earthquake than one that measures 2.0 on 
the Richter scale?
	 For each whole number increase on the Richter scale, approximately 31 times more 
destructive energy is released by the earthquake.
b	 How much more energy would be released by this earthquake in Turkey than one 
measuring 3.0 on the Richter scale?
	 On average, about 120 earthquakes of the size of the one in Turkey occur around the 
world each year.
c	 Complete the sentence: This means that one such earthquake occurs on average every 
_______ days in a year.
7	
In the mid-week lottery there are three divisions. The first division prize of $2.658 million 
was shared between 13 winners. The second division prize of $65 433 was shared between 
43 winners, and the third division prize pool of $11 987 was shared between 104 winners. 
Answer these questions to the nearest dollar.
a	 What was the total prize pool?
b	 How much money did each of the first division winners receive?
c	 How much money did each of the second division winners receive?
d	 How much money did each of the third division winners receive?
e	 The money for the lottery comes from ticket sales. If the government takes 20% of the 
money collected from ticket sales before any prizes are paid out, what was the total 
value of ticket sales in the lottery?
f	 How much money did the government take out?
8	
Finally, the weather. Tomorrow’s minimum 
temperature is forecast to be 13° Celsius, and the 
maximum 24° Celsius. 
	
Convert tomorrow’s minimum and maximum 
temperatures into degrees Fahrenheit. Answer 
correctly to one decimal place.

24 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘What’s it Worth?’ 
11
The team casts its expert eye over various valuables, and tells us exactly what they think they’re 
worth. It’s all about buying price and selling price, and how they change over the years.
Based on a British show, ‘What’s it Worth’ features a team of antique and collectables experts 
who visit shows and exhibitions around the country. The experts look at various objects owned 
by different people and value these objects. Sometimes the owners get a very nice surprise … 
other times, not so nice!
1	
A pair of vases from the 1920s is valued at $950 for the two. The owners had purchased 
them in England five years ago for £120 each. If the exchange rate is one English 
pound for $2.40 Australian, how much more is the pair of vases worth now than when 
purchased? (Answer in $ Australian.)
2	
The ‘What’s it Worth’ experts value a 200-year-old Chinese statue at $28 750. It is made 
of solid gold and weighs 835 g. If gold is worth $790 Australian per ounce, and there 
are 28 grams to an ounce, calculate the value of the gold in the statue (to the nearest 
whole dollar).
3	
An unusual and rare set of rice bowls featuring handpainted Japanese artwork dating 
back to 1907 was presented for valuation.
a	 The original owner of the bowls bought them new, 11 years before they were painted. In 
what year were the bowls made?
b	 If they were sold as individual bowls, the experts estimated they would be worth up to 
$95 each. But sold as a complete set, they are worth up to 55% more than the combined 
cost of the individual pieces. Up to what price could the current owner expect to receive 
for them if they chose to sell them as a set of six bowls?
c	 Suggest why the bowls might be worth more as  
a set.
4	
A fanatical collector of soft drink containers started 
collecting on his 19th birthday. He has just turned 
62.
a	 Over the first 5 years he was collecting, his 
collection grew from zero to 2360 cans and 
bottles. What was the average number of 
containers he collected per year during this time?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
25
‘What’s it Worth?’ (cont’d) 
11
b	 Over the next 22 years, this average figure decreased to 227 containers collected every 
year. Over the 3 years after that, he did not add to his collection. Then he collected 
avidly for the following 4 years, adding another 1929 containers to the collection. 
	 Since then, he has averaged 97 containers per year. If he has never sold or given away 
any containers, what is the total number of containers in his collection now?
5	
An 80-year-old solid blackwood dresser cabinet is auctioned. Its reserve price is set 
at $1800.
a	 What is meant by the reserve price?
b	 Bidding started slowly but became keenly contested by two bidders. The auctioneer 
started taking bids at $1200. There were two $100 bids, followed by seven $50 bids. 
The bidding then increased by $20, and there was a total of six such bids. These were 
followed by three $10 bids, and finally five $5 bids. 
	 What was the final price bid for the dresser?
c	 Did the dresser sell at auction? (That is, was it above or below the reserve price?)
d	 By how much did the dresser exceed or fall short of its reserve price?
e	 What percentage above or below the reserve price was the final bid?
6	
An antique extendable table was valued by the 
experts at $6500. It was a round table with an 
insert that slotted in to increase the size of the 
tabletop. The dimensions of the tabletop and 
insert are shown. 
	
Give answers to 2 decimal places.
a	 What is the area of the round tabletop?
b	 The insert increases the area of the tabletop by 
1.84 m2. What is the total area of the extended 
tabletop with the insert in place?
c	 Calculate x.

Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘Funny Videos Shot at Home’ 
12
The viewers’ own blooper reels – join us for a focus on geometry as misfortune is captured by 
amateur cams.
The thrills, spills and hilarity of those many embarrassing moments that take place every day 
– just make sure someone’s got the video camera handy at the time and the whole country 
ends up sharing it with you …
Unless otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.
1	
How’s this for wheel good fun? When the Jones family went bike riding, Katie got some 
video of her dad riding down a hill on a bicycle – when the wheel fell off, so did her 
dad … ouch!

wheel fell off. What was Dad’s average speed in m/s between A and C until he lost the 
wheel?

decimal place.

Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
‘Cops on the Beat’ 
14
Forget watching people acting as cops – this is the real stuff! TV crews are dispatched with teams of 
police as they crunch the numbers on crime with percentages, money, length and graphing.
This action is definitely not acted. ‘Cops on the Beat’ takes you out on the streets, into homes, 
shops, offices – even down to the waterfront – where every day and night our police are 
confronted with a side of life that most of us only ever imagine.
1	
‘Cops on the Beat’ went with a police team to investigate a suspected stolen car operation 
in the inner city. On arriving at a warehouse, they arrested four men and two women and 
impounded 14 vehicles that had been reported stolen.
a	 The police said the vehicles had an estimated total street value of $290 000. Included 
in the haul was a Porsche worth $105 000. What was the average value of each of the 
other vehicles found in the warehouse (to the nearest whole dollar)?
b	 One of the vehicles had some damage to its right-hand side, which had been caused 
during the theft. The vehicle had an estimated street value of between $16 500 and  
$17 000 but the police said that if it had been sold illegally with the damage, the asking 
price would drop by 30–40%. Using these estimations given by the police, calculate the 
minimum and maximum value of the vehicle had the thieves been able to sell it in its 
damaged state.
c	 This operation was the third of its type that this police investigation unit had uncovered 
in 12 months. The combined total value of all stolen vehicles recovered in the three 
investigations was $1 389 543, but the total value of all vehicles stolen during those 12 
months was estimated at $12 500 000. What percentage of the estimated stolen vehicle 
market has this investigation unit been able to recover over the past year (to 1 decimal 
place)?
2	
Another investigation followed by ‘Cops on the Beat’ was into a fraud carried out by the 
manager of a company. Over the course of two years, she had siphoned off a total of  
$567 000 from customers’ accounts into her own bank accounts for her personal use.
a	 In one account she had operated for nine months, she was collecting 7.2% interest per 
annum. She opened this account with $245 000 and did not add to it. How much was 
in this account when she was caught?

© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007 
Maths in Television 
31
‘Cops on the Beat’ (cont’d) 
14
b	 From one customer, she had regularly taken an 
amount of $17.23 every fortnight. She had done 
this between 1 March and 5 December in the same 
year. How much had she stolen from this customer 
in total?
c	 Of the total $567 000 stolen, she claimed she had 
lost $98 000 gambling. What percentage of the 
total stolen funds is this (to 1 decimal place)?
d	 The police, however, stated that in all 38% of the 
total amount stolen was unaccounted for. How 
much money is this?
e	 Given the woman’s confession about the gambling 
money, how much more money over and above 
this figure could not be traced?
3	
Down to the waterfront – and ‘Cops on the Beat’ are stopping recreational fishing boats to 
check the size of the catch. Large quantities of undersized fish are finding their way onto 
the black market – in particular, King George whiting. Where the police are swooping, the 
legal maximum limit of King George whiting for recreational fishers is 75, and each fish 
must be 30 cm or more in length. During the operation police inspected 68 fishing boats. 
These boats contained a total of 2940 fish of which 1371 were King George whiting. In all, 
160 whiting were found to be undersized. Seven of the boats had more than 75 whiting on 
board.
a	 What was the minimum number of whiting in total that these seven boats could have 
contained?
b	 The seven boats actually contained 1098 whiting between them. What was the average 
number of whiting on board each of those seven boats (to the nearest whole fish)?
c	 The seven boats also accounted for 85% of all the undersized whiting seized. How many 
fish is this?
d	 Do you think there is evidence here that the owners of these seven boats could be 
involved in the illegal sale of whiting? Explain.
4	
One man was caught with 16 King George whiting in all, including two that were 29.7 cm 
and 29.85 cm respectively. The man showed police an old battered steel ruler and claimed 
he used it to measure every fish he caught. The police let him off with a caution.
a	 By what percentage was each of the undersized fish below the legal limit?
b	 Do you think the police treated the man fairly? Why or why not?
c	 What advice might the police have given the man when they cautioned him?

graph or a pie chart to provide a graphic representation of the break down of this data.

uploads/mathematics/Maths in Television/.searchText:
38 
Maths in Television 
© Simon Garner and Blake Education 2007
You shoot two hours of tape and end up using 25 seconds of it. Welcome to a behind-the-scenes look 
at how all that stuff ends up on the cutting room floor, from the hours and minutes down to the 
hundredths of seconds.
Behind the scenes in any commercial or public television studio are many people who work 
on editing and preparing finished programs for broadcast. They use a range of technology to 
process footage shot on film by camera operators. Timing has to be highly accurate, so when 
camera operators shoot film, in or out of the studio, a time code appears on the tape accurate 
to hundredths of a second. Editors can then take the material shot by the camera operators 
and select the bits they want to go into a finished program with a high degree of precision.
To read a time code
Time codes are shown as numbers with colons or points separating them into pairs that show 
the hours : minutes up to 60 : whole seconds up to 60 : tenths and hundredths of seconds. Here 
are some examples:
00 : 00 : 13 : 65 = 13.65 seconds
00 : 07 : 22 : 91 = 7 minutes, 22.91 seconds
01 : 34 : 56 : 79 = 1 hour, 34 minutes, 56.79 seconds
1	
What do these time codes read?
a	 02 : 06 : 17 : 08
b	 00 : 28 : 00 : 00
c	 00 : 00 : 00 : 04
d	 17 : 19 : 45 : 12

With all the channels scrambling for market share, keeping on top of who is watching what is big 
business. The figures are all there - population, sample size and percentages – so you work out what 
they mean.
Ratings are critical to the 
operations of commercial 
television stations. By 
having independent 
assessments made of the 
number of people who 
watch different programs 
on different channels at 
different times each day, 
commercial TV stations, 
particularly free-to-air 
channels, can attract 
advertisers. In effect, 
the television channels 
‘sell their audience’ to 
advertisers.
Ratings data isn’t just about 
how many people watch a 
program. 
It’s about a much bigger demographic picture that enables advertisers to choose the best times 
and locations to run their advertisements. This bigger demographic picture includes the age 
range of these viewers, whether they are metropolitan or rural residents, their occupations and 
general income level.
Ratings agencies recruit households to be part of their data collection. Once a household is 
recruited and some details about its occupants recorded, the monitoring of all TV sets in the 
household is done electronically and the data processed by a ratings agency.
The following activities are based on a simple model of collecting ratings data. Unless 
otherwise indicated, express answers correct to 2 decimal places.

In statistics, the following terms are frequently used when conducting surveys. Briefly 
define each one.
a	 population
b	 sample
c	 sample size
2	
A ratings agency carries out an analysis of TV viewing separately for Australia’s six 
state capital cities, as well as combining the data from the states to provide a national 
analysis. It also carries out analysis of TV viewing in rural and remote areas, although 
the data from the capital cities is the most valuable for TV stations and most advertisers.
a	 Suggest some reasons why the viewing habits in different capital cities are analysed 
separately, as well as an analysis being made for national viewing habits.
b	 Why is the statement made that the data from the capital cities is most valuable for the 
TV stations and most advertisers?

Television’s once-a-year celebrity bash where the industry recognises its best – viewer voting, 
the costs of staying at the top in current affairs, speech timing, logical thinking and catering 
arrangements.
Television’s night of nights is the once-a-year Glitz Awards, where the industry shows off 
its best.

The ‘Best Documentary’ Award went to the ‘One Hour’ 
program for its coverage of the downfall of the government 
in the Wisdom Islands. The ‘One Hour’ team spent 58 days 
in the Wisdom Islands as the events unfolded.
	
The team consisted of three camera operators, two sound technicians, a producer, 
assistant producer, two presenters, two equipment technicians and 12 other staff. In 
dispatching the team to the Wisdom Islands, the cost breakdown was as follows:
•	 wages paid to camera operators and sound technicians = $250/day
•	 wages paid to producer = $300/day
•	 wages paid to assistant producer = $275/day
•	 wages paid to presenters = $400/day
•	 wages paid to equipment technicians = $280/day
•	 wages paid to 12 other staff = $200/day
•	 return flights for each team member = $850
•	 accommodation, meals for each team member = $85/day

‘Best TV Drama’. A total of 92 346 viewers voted in this 
category and the results are shown in the table below.

•	 transport within the Wisdom Islands = $2600 (total for 58 days)

cover the story?
b	 If a budget of $425 000 was set aside for sending the team to the Wisdom Islands, was 
the actual total cost under or over budget? By how much?
3	
All the attendees at the Awards were instructed that if they won an award, the maximum 
time they could spend on a thank-you speech was 45 seconds.
a	 If there were a total of 48 awards made and all speech-makers stuck to their limit, how 
many minutes would the speeches take up over the evening?
b	 One-eighth of the award winners went over the allotted speech time by an average 
of 18.5 seconds each. However, five award winners declined to make any speech, and 
another 14 of them went under the allotted speech time by an average of 11 seconds 
each. What was the actual amount of total speech time on the night? (Answer in 
minutes and seconds.)

The top individual award for the night, the ‘Golden Glitz Award’, was decided between six 
finalists. The runner-up received the ‘Silver Glitz Award’. The finalists were:
J	Lee Tan (Lead male actor in drama series ‘Away from Home’)
J	Ralph Smithers (Host of ‘Ralph Live’)
J	Denzel Elliot (Lead male actor in drama series ‘The Neighbourhood’)
J	Jessica Flaherty (Presenter ‘Time Off’)
J	Rowena Minicelli (Lead female actor in drama series ‘Away from Home’)
J	Colleen O’Brien (Co-host of ‘The Tomorrow Show’)
•	 Lee Tan was the second highest placed male in the ‘Golden Glitz’.
•	 One of the top two awards went to a lead actor in a drama series, but not the other 
top award.
•	 Two females finished lower in the final voting than the lowest placed male.
•	 Ralph Smithers won one of the top two awards last year, but finished one place 
lower in the voting this year.
•	 It was Jessica Flaherty’s first time in the final six, but the person who came fifth had 
also come fifth last year.
Use this information to rank the finalists in order from 1 to 6 and identify the winners of the 
‘Golden Glitz Award’ and ‘Silver Glitz Award’.

Papua New Guinea is home to a large number  
of species of birds. 
The bird-of-paradise is universally identified with the  
island of New Guinea. An adult bird-of-paradise is  
depicted on the national flag of Papua New Guinea.
There are 44 species of birds-of-paradise worldwide  
and 35 species are found in Papua New Guinea.  
A few species are also found in surrounding islands  
and north-eastern Australia.
The smallest bird-of-paradise in size is the  
King Bird-of-paradise which on average has  
a mass of 50 g and is 15 cm long. 
The Curl-crested Manucode is 44 cm long  
and has a mass of 430 g.
The male Black Sicklebill, with its long tail,  
is the longest bird-of-paradise species at 110 cm.
1

birds-of-paradise are found in  
Papua New Guinea?
2 
Express the average mass of a King  
Bird-of-paradise as a fraction of the  
average mass of a Curl-crested Manucode.  
Simplify your answer.
3 
Express the length of a Curl-crested  
Manucode as a fraction of the length of  
a male Black Sicklebill. Simplify your answer. 
4 
Express the length of a King Bird-of-paradise as a percentage of the length  
of a male Black Sicklebill. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
There are many other types of birds found in New Guinea.
The Papuan Eagle (also known as the Kapul Eagle) has an average length of 83 cm.  
Its wingspan measures 157 cm and its average mass is 2 000 g.
The Palm Cockatoo has an average mass of 1 060 g.
5 
a  Express the average mass of a Palm Cockatoo as a fraction of the average mass  
of a Papuan Eagle. Simplify your answer. 
b Write this answer as a percentage.

10 of the length of a Papuan Eagle. 
 
What is the average length of a Palm Cockatoo?  
Answer to the nearest centimetre.

8 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Elephants in Thailand 
3
The Asian elephant is a smaller cousin of the  
African elephant, with relatively smaller ears.  
It is the largest terrestrial mammal in Asia. 
The elephant’s massive size and strength  
made it a reliable beast of burden. It is  
a national symbol of Thailand and has  
served many roles in that country’s  
long history. It has been used in timber  
logging, as a war machine and in  
processions and ceremonies. 
In 2010, it was estimated that only  
about 2 000 wild elephants remained in  
the forests of Thailand. It was estimated  
there were approximately 3 000  
domesticated elephants. 
Today, domesticated elephants are  
more likely to be seen carrying tourists  
or performing in some form of  
entertainment than working in  
the jungle or on farms.
1 
Around 1900 it was estimated that there were at least 100 000 domesticated elephants 
working in Thailand. By 1952, that number had dropped to around 13 400. 
 
In 2010, it was estimated that there were only 3 000 domesticated elephants and  
2 000 wild elephants in Thailand.
 
Express the number of domesticated elephants in Thailand in 2010 as a percentage of 
a the number of domesticated elephants in 1900. 
b the number of domesticated elephants in 1952.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place. 
c the total number of elephants in 2010.
d the number of wild elephants in 2010.
2 
Tan is a mahout (an elephant handler). He is 1.68 m tall and has a mass of 68 kg. 
 
His elephant is 2.8 m tall and has a mass of 4.76 tonnes (4 760 kg).
a Express Tan’s height as a percentage of the height of his elephant. 
b Express Tan’s mass as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
3 
Tan’s elephant eats around 135 kg of plant matter each day. 
 
Express this as a percentage of the mass of his elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
9
Once they are born, baby elephants enjoy a 3 to 5 year childhood before their training begins. 
They learn to push, carry and stack logs as well as how to walk in a procession.  
Working elephants have a career of about 50 years. 
4 
Tan began training his elephant when it was 4 years old.  
The training took 5 years.  
Tan and the elephant then began work.  
His elephant is now 25 years old.
a How many years has the elephant been working? 
b What percentage of its life did the elephant spend in training? 
c What percentage of the elephant’s life has it been working? 
5 
The law in Thailand requires working elephants to be retired at age 61 after working  
for 50 years. They are usually released into the wild. 
 
An elephant at a sanctuary is 72 years old. 
 
What percentage of its life did the elephant spend working?  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
Each year, the town of Surin in north-eastern Thailand hosts an Elephant Round-up Festival. 
More than 300 domesticated elephants are brought to the town by their mahouts.  
The festival lasts 10 days. The elephants demonstrate their skills and participate in parades 
and battle re-enactments. 
6 
The average elephant drinks 160 litres of water each day. 
a How many kilolitres of water are needed for each elephant for 10 days? 
b How many kilolitres of water are needed for 300 elephants for 10 days? 
7 
The average elephant has a mass of 4 800 kg.  
It eats 130 kg of plants and vegetables each day. 
a What is the total mass of plants and vegetables the average elephant will eat  
during the 10 days of the festival?  
b Express this as a percentage of the mass of the elephant.  
Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
8 
A female elephant stands 2.3 metres in height and has a normal mass of 3.2 tonnes  
(3 200 kg). She gave birth to a baby. Shortly after birth, the baby stood 90 centimetres 
high and had a mass of 90 kg.
a Express the baby’s height as a percentage of its mother’s height.  
Answer correct to the nearest whole number.
b Express the baby’s mass as a percentage of its mother’s mass.  
Answer correct to one decimal place.
9 
A male elephant has a mass of 3.4 tonnes.  
Its brain has a mass of 5 kg. Express this as a percentage of the elephant’s mass.  
Answer correct to two decimal places.

10 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014
Japan’s high speed trains are called 
Shinkansen (bullet trains). The first 
bullet train was operated between 
Tokyo and Osaka in 1964, the year the 
Olympic Games were held in Tokyo. 
Today bullet trains run between many 
cities in Japan. On some lines, trains 
run every 5 to 10 minutes.
The fastest trains are called ‘Nozomi’. 
They connect major cities like Tokyo, 
Nagoya, Osaka and Hiroshima, 
making few stops in between. 
1 
A Nozomi train leaves Tokyo at 7:50 am and arrives at Shin-Osaka at 10:29 am.  
It makes only 4 stops in the 552 kilometre journey. 
 
How long does the journey take?  
Answer in hours and minutes.
2 
A slower Hikari train leaves Tokyo at 9:33 am and arrives at Shin-Osaka at 12:30 pm.  
It makes 6 stops between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka.
a How long does the journey take? Answer in hours and minutes.
b Convert your answer to hours, correct to 2 decimal places.
3 
A Nozomi train leaves Kyoto at 3:45 pm. The 380 kilometre journey to Hiroshima takes 
1 hour and 36 minutes. At what time does this train arrive in Hiroshima? 
4 
A train takes 2 hours 18 minutes to travel from Tokyo to Kyoto,  
a distance of 513 kilometres.
a Convert the time to hours. Give your answer as a decimal. 
b Use the rule: Speed = Distance 
Time
 to calculate the average speed of the train, correct to  
1 decimal place.
5 
A train takes 1 hour 25 minutes to travel from Tokyo to Nagano,  
a distance of 222 kilometres.
a Convert the time to hours, correct to 2 decimal places. 
b Calculate the average speed of the train, correct to 1 decimal place. 
Bullet trains in Japan 
4
In the following questions you will need the rule:
Average speed = distance travelled ÷ time taken or Speed = Distance 
Time
ISBN   978 1 92571 065 6

© Paul Steenson and Blake Education 2014 
Maths in the Asia Pacific 
11
6 
A train takes 3 hours 10 minutes to travel  
from Hiroshima to Nagasaki, a distance  
of 434 kilometres.
a Convert the time to hours, correct to  
2 decimal places.
b Calculate the average speed of the train,  
correct to 1 decimal place.
7 
A train travelled between Tokyo and Karuizawa in 1 hour and 3 minutes.  
It had an average speed of 139.8 km/h for the journey.
a How many hours did the journey take? Give your answer as a decimal.
b What is the distance between Tokyo and Karuizawa, to the nearest kilometre?
8 
A train left Hiroshima at 9:10 am. It travelled at an average speed of 215.4 km/h  
and arrived at Tokyo at 1:19 pm.
a How many hours did the journey take?  
Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
b What is the distance between Hiroshima and Tokyo, to the nearest kilometre?
9 
A train travelled between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka at an average speed of 215 km/h.  
The two stations are 552 km apart. How long did the journey take?  
Give your answer to the nearest minute.
10 The distance between Tokyo and Sendai is 351.8 km.  
A ‘Hayabusa’ train completed the journey at an average speed of 219 km/h.  
How long did the journey take?  
Give your answer to the nearest minute. 
 
11 The distance between Shin-Aomori and Tokyo is 713.7 km.  
A train departed Shin-Aomori at 10:35 am and travelled to Tokyo  
at an average speed of 203.9 km/h. 
a How long did the journey take?  
Give your answer to the nearest minute.
b At what time did this train arrive at Tokyo?
Bullet trains in Japan (cont’d) 
4
The rule: Speed = Distance 
Time
 
can be rearranged when you want  
to calculate the distance travelled  
or the time taken.
Distance = Speed × Time and 
Time taken = Distance travelled ÷ Speed

Justine and Melissa were visiting 
Vietnam. They saw many street 
markets where fresh fruit and 
vegetables were sold. The prices were 
all marked in the local currency. The 
local money is known as Vietnamese 
dong (VND). The prices looked 
very high. However, the exchange 
rate was one Australian dollar was 
approximately equal to 21 000 VND.
1 
Justine decided to buy some fruit. 
The prices were based on one 
kilogram. Justine purchased: 
a Calculate the cost of each item.
b Calculate the total cost of Justine’s purchase. 
c Justine paid using a 50 000 VND note. How much change should she receive?
2 
The next day Melissa purchased: 
a Calculate the cost of each item.
b Calculate the total cost of Melissa’s purchase. 
c Melissa gave the vendor 80 000 VND. How much change should she receive?
3 
Their friend Mrs Linh was doing her shopping. She purchased:
 
Calculate the total cost of Mrs Linh’s shopping.
Local markets

200 grams of morning glory @ 25 000 VND per kg
900 grams of mangoes @ 30 000 VND per kg 
700 grams of lychees @ 50 000 VND per kg

4 
The currency exchange rate was one Australian dollar was approximately  
equal to 21 000 VND. To convert from Vietnamese dong to Australian dollars,  
you divide by 21 000.
 
Use this rate to convert these amounts to Australian dollars.  
Answer to the nearest cent.
a 25 000 VND 
b 40 000 VND
c 60 000 VND
d 75 000 VND
e 100 000 VND
f 130 000 VND
g 170 000 VND
h 250 000 VND
5 
Convert the total cost of Justine’s purchase (Question 1) to Australian dollars.
6 
Convert the total cost of Melissa’s purchase (Question 2) to Australian dollars.
7 
Convert the total cost of Mrs Linh’s purchase (Question 3) to Australian dollars.
8 
Thang was buying fruit for his family. He purchased:
a Calculate the total cost of Thang’s  
shopping in VND.
b Convert your answer to Australian  
dollars. Answer to the nearest cent.
9 
Justine saw a woman selling  
flowers from a bicycle. She decided  
to purchase some flowers to give  
to Mrs Linh. The flowers cost  
65 000 VND. Convert this amount  
to Australian dollars.
Local markets (cont’d)

Matthew was reading about some of the  
tall buildings in Asia. 
The Jin Mao Tower in Shanghai (China)  
is 420 metres high. 
The Petronas Twin Towers in Kuala Lumpur 
(Malaysia) is 452 metres high.
Taipei 101 in the capital of Taiwan  
is 509 metres high.
Matthew wanted to compare the heights  
of these buildings with the heights of the 
Eureka Tower in Melbourne (297 metres high) 
and Q1 on the Queensland Gold Coast  
(323 metres high).
First, he constructed a column graph of  
the heights.

c Express the mass of Taipei 101 as a fraction of the mass of the Eureka Tower.
